title: Take-Two Interactive files subpoenas against Microsoft, Discord, and X amid ongoing GTA 6 leaks
author: Sophie McEvoy
content:
Take-Two Interactive has subpoenaed Microsoft, Discord, and X regarding the ongoing Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks.
As Kotaku and IGN report, Rockstar Games' parent company is asking the companies to provide "any records related to various online accounts involved in posting and sharing leaks." This includes user data as well as linked OneDrive and Xbox accounts.
As written in a subpoena filed with the Southern District of New York last Thursday (August 20), Take-Two is looking "to obtain the identity of an alleged infringer or infringers, and that such information will only be used for the purpose of protecting Take Two's rights."
"The copyrighted material includes but is not limited to audiovisual content, artwork, images, dialogue, or other creative elements."
The petition also cites a GitHub repository, owned by Microsoft, where leaked content was posted.
Take-Two has requested that "all internal Microsoft business records and investigative records associated with Microsoft's internal investigation of the 'CyberLeek' persona sufficient to identify the user(s), person(s) and/or entity/ies associated with that persona."
As for Discord, Take-Two has requested "all identifying information associated with all user accounts that are/were members communicating with the Discord server(s) listed below during the time period from June 1, 2026 to present; and for those accounts, provide any associated device/telemetry records where one or more of the tool/file artefacts below were present on the system."
This includes "the account ID, registration email, registration and last-login IP addresses, phone number, linked connections (Google/Xbox/etc.), any associated device identifiers (MachineGuild/MSA), and content related to Grand Theft Auto ('GTA'), Rockstar, or CyberLeek from their OneDrive account."
Microsoft and Discord must produce all related documents by September 4, 2026.
One of the subpoenas also includes a copy of a take-down request issued to Discord (via Mashable), which reads:
"The reported post contains unauthorised, leaked gameplay footage from the unreleased game Grand Theft Auto 6. This material reproduces our Client's copyrighted, unreleased game assets and was published and distributed without any authorisation from the copyright holder. The content is presented as genuine leaked Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay from Take-Two Interactive Software, Inc., and its distribution constitutes unauthorised reproduction and public disclosure of our Client's copyrighted work."
Discord stated on Friday that it will "review and comply with valid subpoenas" when received.
Xbox chief technology officer Scott Van Vliet said on social media that the company is "working closely with Take-Two and Rockstar Games to support efforts to protect creative works and intellectual property."
Last week, a hacker group began posting daily leaks of apparent GTA 6 details and footage. The group, known as "CyberLeek," has threatened to release new videos daily.
This comes ahead of Rockstar's extended look at the game, which will premiere on Netflix this Friday, August 28.
Take-Two CEO Strauss Zelnick previously told GamesIndustry.biz this partnership is merely "one of the hors d'oeuvres" of its marketing campaign for the game, which launches on November 19.
summary: Take-Two Interactive has filed subpoenas against Microsoft, Discord, and X to identify users responsible for leaking unreleased Grand Theft Auto 6 content. The legal action seeks user data, internal investigation records regarding the 'CyberLeek' persona, and linked accounts to protect the company's copyrighted material. Microsoft and Discord are required to produce the requested documents by September 4, 2026.
key_points: Take-Two Interactive subpoenaed Microsoft, Discord, and X over ongoing GTA 6 leaks.
The subpoenas demand user data, registration details, IP addresses, and records related to the 'CyberLeek' persona.
Microsoft and Discord must produce the requested documents by September 4, 2026.
Discord stated it will comply with valid subpoenas, and Xbox CTO Scott Van Vliet confirmed cooperation with Take-Two and Rockstar Games.

title: Android Pulse app may already be on your phone, and now we know what it does
author: Shimul Sood
content:
Android Pulse app may already be on your phone, and now we know what it does
Aug 24, 2026 — 4:32 AM ET
![Android Pulse app update on Google Pixel 11 Android Pulse app update on Google Pixel 11](https://www.androidauthority.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Android-Pulse-app-update-on-Google-Pixel-11.jpg)
- Google’s Android Pulse app is starting to appear as an available update in the Play Store.
- The background service appears to detect unusual resource usage, such as apps suddenly consuming too much battery, memory, or processing power.
- Android Pulse isn’t new; builds date back to March, and the Play Store shows more than 10 million downloads.
There are plenty of Google apps you probably use every day, but Android Pulse is definitely not one of them. In fact, you may not even know it exists. That could change soon, though, because this mysterious system app is suddenly showing up as an available update in the Play Store.
As first spotted by 9to5Google, Android Pulse is a Google-made app that works behind the scenes. Its job appears to be pretty simple: keep an eye out for apps or parts of Android that are using your phone’s resources in unusual ways.
Google, unsurprisingly, describes this in much less exciting terms. The Play Store listing says Android Pulse helps distribute rules for detecting anomalies related to “critical system resource consumption.”
Say an app goes rogue overnight and suddenly starts draining your battery, or something running in the background begins eating up far more memory or processing power than it normally should. Android Pulse appears designed to help Android recognize those unusual spikes. You won’t be opening Pulse to run a scan yourself, but what it does behind the scenes could eventually help Google catch problematic behavior faster.
And that’s what makes Android Pulse worth paying attention to. Battery drain, overheating, and badly behaved background apps are some of those Android problems that can be incredibly annoying because figuring out what is causing them isn’t always easy. If Google can get better at spotting these anomalies before they turn into bigger problems, that could ultimately mean a more stable Android experience for everyone.
Despite only now becoming more visible, Android Pulse itself isn’t particularly new. APKMirror has versions of the app dating back to March, with several builds appearing since then. Its Play Store listing also shows more than 10 million downloads, so there’s a good chance it’s already been sitting on millions of phones without anyone paying much attention.
There’s at least one small visual clue explaining the name. The App info page displays a green icon resembling a heartbeat or pulse reading — it’s fitting for an app that essentially seems to be checking Android’s vitals.
The interesting part is that you can now actually encounter Android Pulse while checking for app updates yourself. Open the Play Store, tap your profile picture, head to Manage apps & device, and tap Manage. From there, select Updates available, and Android Pulse may be sitting alongside all the regular apps waiting to be updated.
For most people, Android Pulse probably isn’t something you’ll ever need to open or interact with directly. Instead, its sudden appearance in the Play Store gives us a rare look at one of the many services working in the background on Android. And if it can help Google better identify apps or system processes that are draining your battery, hogging memory, or otherwise misbehaving, that could ultimately make Android a little more reliable without you having to do anything at all.
summary: The Google-made Android Pulse app is appearing as an available update in the Play Store, though it is not a new application and already has over 10 million downloads. Operating as a background service, the system app is designed to detect unusual resource usage like battery drain, excessive memory consumption, and high processing power. Users cannot manually open the app to run scans, but its background monitoring aims to help Google identify problematic behavior and improve overall Android stability.
key_points: Android Pulse is a Google background system app that is now appearing as an available update in the Play Store.
The app's primary function is to detect unusual resource consumption, such as apps draining battery, memory, or processing power.
Builds of the app date back to March, and it already has more than 10 million downloads on devices.
Users do not interact with or open the app directly, as it operates silently to help catch problematic behavior and improve Android stability.

title: iPhone Fold Release Date: Apple’s Perfect Timing
author: Janhoi McGregor
content:
Apple’s upcoming iPhone Fold is walking into a foldable phone market that is the most vibrant it has ever been, according to new research. Coupled with the success of the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and its unusual design, the iPhone Fold couldn't have better timing.
But that doesn’t guarantee success, because foldable phones, especially high-priced first-generation ones, come with real challenges that don’t exist for regular slab phones.
iPhone Fold Enters A Market That Is Booming
New data from Omdia forecasts the global foldable market will grow more than 20% annually through 2028, hitting 36 million units. In the first half of 2026 alone, 5.1 million foldable phones shipped. Clamshell foldables (flip phones) saw shipments collapse 47% year-on-year.
Book-style devices, the kind Apple is making and like the Galaxy Z Fold 8, now account for 69% of all foldable shipments. Counterpoint Research's Enze Qi put it plainly: "In-fold has moved from a secondary form factor to the mainstream."
The good news doesn't stop there. The Galaxy Z Fold 8 recorded 1.44 million pre-orders in seven days in South Korea alone, breaking Samsung's own all-time record. 70% of those buyers chose the new wide format over the tall-shaped Ultra.
As I reported earlier this month, Samsung has since ordered 1 million additional units to meet demand. That is the clearest possible signal that the squat, 4:3 book-style foldable has mass appeal. By luck or some excellent planning, Apple chose the same shape for the iPhone Fold.
If the leaks are correct and Apple is indeed planning to produce 10 million units, which is more than three times Samsung’s initial order of 2.8 million, we will likely see this style of foldable phone become not only wildly popular, but also mainstream.
The iPhone Fold Will Face Some Big Challenges
None of this means the iPhone Fold will succeed, though, because foldable phones are notoriously complex, especially at scale.
Apple is doing this for the first time, so it has to hope that the hinge holds up across the millions of different ways it will be used and flexed. The foldable UI also needs to be smooth from the start. It took Samsung years to get this right after some janky early iterations that struggled with app-resizing and multitasking.
There's also the cost. If analyst predictions prove correct and the iPhone Fold tops out at $2,400, Apple will have to find a way to make that enticing through pre-order deals and high trade-in prices.
There’s also the repair issue. Foldable displays are expensive to replace, which may put some buyers off. Battery life, too, could be a concern for regular iPhone buyers who aren't used to how quickly powering two and a half screens can drain a cell.
But the excitement for wide foldable phones can't be ignored, nor can the growing interest in foldables more broadly. Both suggest Apple is making the iPhone Fold at the best possible time. We'll just have to see if it can make a device that is as good as its timing.
summary: Apple is entering a booming foldable phone market with its upcoming iPhone Fold, benefiting from strong consumer interest in book-style foldables like the successful Galaxy Z Fold 8. However, the device will face significant challenges, including manufacturing complexity, high pricing up to $2,400, costly repairs, and battery life concerns. Despite these obstacles, the growing mainstream popularity of wide format foldables suggests Apple's timing for the release is ideal.
key_points: The global foldable market is forecast to grow over 20% annually through 2028, reaching 36 million units.
Book-style devices account for 69% of all foldable shipments, with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 breaking pre-order records in South Korea.
Apple has reportedly planned to produce 10 million units of the iPhone Fold using a similar squat, 4:3 book-style format.
The iPhone Fold faces potential hurdles such as first-generation manufacturing complexity, a high predicted price of $2,400, expensive repairs, and battery drain.
Foldable user interfaces must be smooth from launch, a challenge that took Samsung years to master.

title: 'Security by antiquity': Why older tech is sometimes safer from hackers
author: Chris Baraniuk
content:
'Security by antiquity': Why older tech is sometimes safer from hackers
![Alamy Nokia 9210 phone (Credit: Alamy)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5ppng.jpg.webp) Alamy
The fear of hacking has made some people turn to other forms of technology ignored by new generations of cyber criminals.
You might not expect a world-renowned cyber security expert to rely on old, potentially vulnerable email software. But, for years, that's what Mikko Hyppönen did. Shunning mainstream options such as Hotmail and Gmail, he instead chose obsolete email software called Eudora.
"I used to run it years after it was out of [technical] support," says Hyppönen, a Finnish computer security expert.
He preferred Eudora for various reasons, arguing it was "really superior in many ways". Although Eudora was far from perfectly secure, as people switched to newer email tools, Hyppönen realised that hackers were forgetting about Eudora.
Hyppönen calls it "security by antiquity". Others use the phrase "security by obsolescence" and in both cases this means relying on an older technology or system since it may prove, somewhat counterintuitively, safer than more recent alternatives.
While Hyppönen stresses that using the latest, fully patched and updated software is still "the optimum situation", there are specific cases where older tech could be preferable from a security standpoint.
"The vast majority of attackers are criminals trying to make money and it doesn't make any sense for them to target systems being run by 50 people," he explains.
![Getty Images Global positioning system (GPS) handsets like these in use by the Ukrainian armed forces are vulnerable to electronic jamming (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5ppqd.jpg.webp) Getty Images
Hyppönen isn't alone. The Irish Aviation Authority, for instance, recently decided to keep ground-based radio navigation beacons in use because supposedly the more modern satellite-based global positioning system (GPS) has proven so susceptible to jamming in recent years.
"Security by antiquity" is, it turns out, a quiet way of beating cyber-criminals, hackers and enemy attackers.
Matt Bishop, a computer scientist and professor emeritus at the University of California, Davis, has tested this principle, somewhat by accident. Back in the 1990s, he and his colleagues set up a system connected to the internet and deliberately left it accessible so that they could catch hackers and bots attempting to breach it. This is a common cyber-security research technique known as a honeypot – a kind of trap set up in carefully controlled conditions.
But the team picked an older software version for their honeypot that had been upgraded multiple times since its release and, consequently, no hackers bothered to target it. "When we upgraded it to the new one, we had all the attacks we wanted," recalls Bishop. "I thought it was so amusing."
This possibility of evading nefarious activity by sticking to old tech can take many forms. Both Bishop and Hyppönen say they have friends who refuse to get a smartphone. "One person I know [uses] a Nokia 9210," says Hyppönen, referring to a simple, "dumb" mobile phone first released 25 years ago.
While hackers can't target it in quite the same way they might target a modern Android or iOS device, the phone's operating system, Symbian, does have some old, known vulnerabilities. The flipside is that "nobody's targeting them anymore", adds Hyppönen. Similarly, the Nokia could be more at risk from techniques that snoop on phone calls. But how many people will bother? It's a security trade-off.
As technology has advanced, experts have often questioned whether the latest systems are actually more risky than older ones. During the late 1990s, Bishop wrote a speech in which he argued that computers were "considerably less secure than the paper systems we still use, and that are rapidly being replaced".
Concerns about the shift from paper to digital technologies remain prevalent, especially when it comes to electronic voting systems. Some say electronic voting machines are desirable partly because they produce election results much more quickly than paper-based systems. That's not enough to sway others, though.
"Voting is the bedrock of our democracy," says Hyppönen. "It's one of the last things I'd like to weaken in any way, especially if the benefits are so small."
Militaries are also known for being reluctant to take chances. Even the world's most active militaries are known to occasionally rely on old technologies for reasons of reliability and security. "One thing I've seen in places like Ukraine is the use of paper maps, or laminated maps, and compasses," says Thomas Withington, associate fellow at the Royal United Services Institute, a think tank. "You can't jam that." It's a kind of "analogue resilience", he adds.
![Getty Images Concerns over the vulnerability of some electronic voting systems mean many elections are still carried out with paper forms (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5ppyt.jpg.webp) Getty Images
Jamming attacks hitting GPS-based navigation have forced some countries to make careful choices about which legacy technologies to retain, and which GPS alternatives to invest in, says Victor Tasiemski, a systems engineer at Overlook Systems Technologies, which works on navigation tech.
That's exactly what happened in Ireland, where a programme to replace ground-based radio beacons has been slowed down in order to keep those beacons operating for longer. A spokeswoman for the Irish Aviation Authority told the Irish Times in June that the beacons were being retained "as part of a planned resilience strategy".
Technologists who work with militaries are familiar with the challenge of designing systems that can link old and new technologies together. Stefan Kraus is co-founder and chief technical officer of Kraus Hamdani Aerospace, which has designed a drone-based communications platform that can connect military personnel to one another, no matter whether they are using older radios or newer ones. Military radio tech that has been around for decades is "tried, tested and secure", he says. "The US military isn't going away from that."
Tasiemski notes that one alternative to GPS-based navigation is eLoran, a radio-based navigation system that has its roots in military technology first developed during World War Two. With attacks targeting GPS systems, eLoran is arguably becoming increasingly desirable, says Tasiemski, because it uses a much more powerful signal and is therefore much trickier to jam: "Overpowering a one-megawatt transmitter is pretty hard."
Robustness is not easy to replace. This applies in the world of data storage, too, where magnetic tape – invented during the 1950s – still plays a huge role today. Companies, research institutions and government agencies continue to store vast amounts of data on reels of tape. The technology has improved significantly since it first appeared, with data storage densities having increased exponentially over the decades.
But the principle remains the same: spools of tape that hold information. The tape can be detached from computer systems, packaged, and transported to secure facilities, including difficult-to-breach underground caverns and repurposed mines.
![Getty Images Reel-to-reel tape is making a comeback because companies see it as a cheaper wave of saving material than computer memory (Credit: Getty Images)](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/images/ic/480xn/p0p5pq18.jpg.webp) Getty Images
"Ransomware is what, for me, kept tape in business the past 10 to 15 years," says Hugues Meyrath, chief executive of Quantum, a company that specialises in data storage.
An organisation locked out of its own computer systems may still be able to retrieve its most important data if staff have made good back-ups, for example on magnetic tape. Interest in magnetic tape is only increasing further today because the cost of random access memory (Ram), a form of computer memory that doesn't rely on tape, is skyrocketing. Meyrath says his company's clients use tape to store all kinds of data – from broadcasters' footage of baseball games to genomes mapped in detail by research facilities.
More like this:
Tape's security attributes stem partly from the fact that most people don't tend to interact with it at all. It's obscure, clunky, old-school tech. "One way to attack a system is to rig a set of USB sticks and throw them around a parking lot," says Bishop, referring to the likelihood that someone will eventually pick up one of the USB sticks and insert it into their computer – a simple way to perpetrate a hack. As he puts it: "You'll never see magnetic tape thrown around a parking lot."
Experts who spoke to the BBC still recommend that people use the latest and most up-to-date technologies for everyday tasks, as it remains the safest approach. But it is worth acknowledging that "new" doesn't necessarily mean "best" in all scenarios. And knowing when and how to switch to older systems could become increasingly important, as cyber-attacks and other threats get more sophisticated.
Withington points again to Ukraine, where Russia has interfered with satellite communications and where GPS navigation has succumbed to significant jamming. Nowhere is "analogue resilience" more prized. "What do people do," asks Withington, "if there's no access to the technology they take for granted?"
--
For more insights, sign up to our Tech Decoded newsletter, where Lily Jamali and Thomas Germain break down the biggest stories of the tech world, and help you live a better digital life. Sign up for free here.
summary: Older technologies can sometimes provide better security or resilience against modern cyberattacks and electronic interference simply because hackers and criminals ignore them. While fully patched, up-to-date software remains the best general practice, various sectors—including aviation, military operations, and data storage—rely on legacy tools like paper maps, old email software, and magnetic tape to avoid digital vulnerabilities. This concept, known as "security by antiquity" or "analogue resilience," highlights how obsolescence can occasionally protect systems from targeted attacks.
key_points: Cybercriminals primarily target mainstream, modern systems to maximize financial gain, often overlooking older or obsolete software.
Organizations like the Irish Aviation Authority and military units in Ukraine retain legacy tools such as radio beacons and paper maps to avoid GPS jamming and digital interference.
Researchers testing honeypots found that older software versions attracted significantly fewer attacks than newly upgraded systems.
Magnetic tape remains widely used for secure data back-ups because it is physically isolated from networks and largely immune to ransomware.
Experts emphasize that while new technology is best for everyday tasks, understanding the benefits of older systems offers a viable trade-off for specific security challenges.

title: Crewe Cut: flat out in the lightest Bentley in 85 years
author: Jethro Bovingdon Published
content:
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/images/news-article/2026/08/79060c1ccd42e1cfbda2dec615aae81d/545977_Honda_Civic_Type_R_-_All_Generations.jpg?w=405&h=228)
Crewe Cut: flat out in the lightest Bentley in 85 years
The Conti GT just got serious: 500kg dropped, no hybrid gubbins and rear-drive. We need spare tyres...
Bentley and all action hero/lunatic/gymkhana god/motocross rider Travis Pastrana wouldn’t usually be two entities with a huge amount in common. Except, I guess, that Pastrana has a metal chassis supporting his frame after many and varied accidents.
So, it’s a mark of the departure signalled by the new Supersports that Bentley chose to launch it with a video featuring Pastrana at the wheel, a great deal of tyre smoke and even a hydraulic handbrake. A drift Bentley? Well, it would appear so.
But, surely, that was just a publicity stunt? Well, yeah. A pretty good one, too. However, when I roll onto the apron of the Top Gear test track there’s a new Bentley Supersports – looking pretty spectacular in Electric Blue, I have to say – and a Pirelli van full to bursting with tyres. The message is clear: this is a Bentley unlike any other. Go and enjoy yourself.
Photography: Mark Riccioni
You might like
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/images/news-article/2026/08/79060c1ccd42e1cfbda2dec615aae81d/545977_Honda_Civic_Type_R_-_All_Generations.jpg?w=405&h=228)
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/images/cars-road-test/2026/08/d7ef49cbac1747cf86b5f8f32ccf77be/1-Toyota-Tundra-TRD-review-2026-US.jpg?w=405&h=228)
Toyota Tundra TRD Pro (US) review: go for the gold
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/images/big-read/2026/07/37548ead546ed28291f7a04ed209cc62/Ariel%20Atom%204RR%20Vs%20Nichols%20N1A.jpg?w=405&h=228)
Battle of the lightweights: Ariel Atom 4RR Vs Nichols N1A
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/images/big-read/2026/08/564c0ccba5a1d9f79ace5ae846e25107/ACT_1018_09735_HR.jpg?w=405&h=228)
Alpine A290 vs Skoda Fabia 130: the battle of the... slightly warm hatches
So, forget everything you know about the Continental GT. The Supersports has ripped up the formula and its specification, positioning and attitude seems more Porsche than Bentley. By ditching the hybrid system of the standard car, reconfiguring the drivetrain to rear-wheel drive, the interior to a strict two-seater, and employing carbon fibre wherever possible, it’s cut over 500kg of mass.
Let me say that again. Over five hundred kilograms. That’s an entire Caterham Seven. Or nearly six average UK male adults. Or one star of My Half Ton Life. No lightweight special edition I can remember has cut this much flab. Admittedly, not many lightweight specials start with a donor car that weighs 2,500kg...
The end result is the lightest Bentley in 85 years, at a shade under 2,000kg. That might not sound featherweight, but in the context of a BMW M5 that weighs 2,435kg or an RS5 Avant at a whopping 2,370kg, it’s borderline miraculous. Of course, ditching the hybrid tech does mean a penalty in terms of power compared to the Continental GT Speed.
The Supersports produces 657bhp and 590lb ft from its 4.0-litre twin turbocharged V8 versus the Speed’s 771bhp and 738lb ft. Even so, it’s capable of 0–62mph in 3.7 seconds and a top speed of 192mph. Plus, the pure acceleration numbers don’t even tell half the story.
Perhaps it’s more relevant and telling that the Supersports can be delivered on Pirelli P Zero Trofeo RS tyres for up to 1.3g of lateral load in the corners. I’ve never heard Bentley talking gs in the past.
Just 500 will be made starting from £343,900. The Supersports isn’t just a cash grab limited edition, though. Bentley says it’s the very start of a new direction for the company, which wants to stretch the brand and the models as far as possible. This is a pretty hardcore exercise, but it’s just the beginning. Except that when you have a history as long as Bentley’s, nothing is truly new.
![Bentley](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/styles/media_embed/public/2026/08/DSC05327.jpg?itok=4q3sX8p-) 
Parked just to the side of that Pirelli van is something extraordinary. Known as ‘Smoky’ it’s effectively a hot rodded version of the original Super Sports from 1925, which was the fastest 3.0-litre model available. In fact, it was the first car that W.O. Bentley would guarantee to hit 100mph with its 80bhp engine. What a way to stand behind your product over a century ago.
Smoky, number 12 of 18 cars, is even more special as its second owner, Kit Baker-Carr, upgraded the engine in 1932 to a 4.5-litre unit and then created a lower body in ’34 before racing the car extensively and with great success at Brooklands. Oh, and if that’s not enough cool history for you, that 4.5-litre engine I mentioned is known as EXP5 and powered the Le Mans-winning Bentley in 1928. In race tune it’s good for 130bhp and an unspecified top speed that I’m very unwilling to ascertain.
Driving it (briefly) is fascinating, discombobulating thanks to a centre throttle pedal, and deeply challenging due to its crash ’box. Did I say challenging? I meant ‘bloody frustrating’. Turns out synchromesh is a very good thing. It’s a deeply cool experience, though. And a reminder that Bentley’s origin story is intertwined with the birth and formative years of motorsport itself.
Top Gear
Newsletter
Get all the latest news, reviews and exclusives, direct to your inbox.
In that context, the new Supersports seems a more natural exploration of Bentley’s most dynamic side. It’s gone for it, that’s for sure. The Supersports features a carbon fibre roof to lower the centre of gravity, carbon fibre lower bumper with integrated front splitter, stacked dive planes on each side, B-shaped ‘fender blades’ just behind the front wheels, plus a rear diffuser and fixed, near-vertical rear spoiler mounted on a new rear bumper with venting for the wheelarches. The result is 300kg of downforce and a pretty dramatic new look.
Forged 22in alloy wheels by Manthey Racing, which is part owned by Porsche and runs its racecars in the World Endurance Championship as well as creating hyper-focused MR kits for the GT3 and GT3 RS, save yet more weight. The Supersports is the first Bentley entirely overseen by Dr Frank-Steffen Walliser, formerly of Porsche and a man who loves a GT3. You can feel that influence from the Manthey wheels all the way up. Of course, you don’t have to be GT3 literate to realise that deleting the rear seats isn’t a bad way to save a few kilos and dial up the attitude.
Incredibly there’s much, much more: a 16mm wider rear track, new twin-chamber dampers, reconfigured traction and stability control and drive modes, punchier shifts and uprated hardware for the eight-speed dual-clutch gearbox, and so the list goes on. However, the Supersports does retain rear-wheel steering for maximum agility and the 48v active anti-roll bars as seen on lesser (morer?) Continental GTs.
Bloody hell? Is it even a Bentley at all?
There’s also an e-LSD to help manage the balance and give the rear tyres a fighting chance of survival against the onslaught of the 4.0-litre engine’s thunderous power. Incidentally, the engine is much modified with a stronger crank, uprated cylinder heads and bigger turbos. There’s also a full length titanium Akrapovič exhaust.
Bloody hell, right? Is it even a Bentley at all? Well, strangely, yes. The seats might have more side bolstering and sit a little lower, but they’re still 11-way adjustable, heated and beautifully trimmed. The interior remains a thing of precise, opulent luxury dripping in fine hides, diamond brushed aluminium and tactile delight. Nobody does interiors quite like Bentley and the Supersports might feel a little more focused but it’s still somewhere you’d be happy to sit for hours on end. Bentley is at pains to point out this particular car is a pre-production prototype, but the quality remains out of this world.
So far, so familiar. However, when you start the engine and begin to move the differences are immediately apparent. The engine really has found its voice. It crackles to life but once under way the volume and intensity is very well judged. The sound is deep, purposeful and just enough to trigger your brain to think ‘phwoar’ without tripping over into comedy quasi-NASCAR vibes like some hardcore Mercedes, for example. Restrained exuberance, you might call it.
![Bentley Supersports](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/styles/media_embed/public/2026/08/DSC06152.jpg?itok=eHVeSScE) 
More impressive still is the transformation in dynamics. The steering feels a little lighter with more clarity, but the sense of agility, the turn-in response and simply the appetite for really attacking corners is all new. On the Trofeo RS tyres the Supersports is extremely sharp, shows brilliant body control and stays poised mid corner in a way no Continental GT has ever done before.
Even in Touring mode the Supersports is intended to align with a Continental GT Speed in Sport, but here there’s another two modes to unlock more character, performance and excitement. For this track-only drive we quickly skip from Touring, through ‘Bentley’ and onto Sport. I think my finger slipped to disable the reconfigured traction control, too. Well, there’s only a decaying Boeing 747 to hit here and I reckon the Supersports would win that fight…
Let loose, the Supersports is a real entertainer. Its front wheels are pinned to the apex and the long wheelbase, monster engine and delicious poise allow you to pick your line and angle of attack with precision and absolute trust. It’s such an easy car to slide around, even for those not blessed with Pastrana’s talent. To be completely fair, the most recent Continental GT with hybrid powertrain is superb fun and so much more fluid, adjustable and playful than ever before.
It’s a hell of a sports car
Here though, there’s a massive increase in responsiveness, control and grip allied to the same indulgent balance. Of course it feels heavy compared to, say, a GT3 or even 911 Turbo. Of course it doesn’t quite have the natural athleticism of an Aston Martin Vantage. But it’s a hell of a sports car when you consider it’s not really a sports car at all.
There are some weaknesses. For me, the dual-clutch gearbox doesn’t go far enough. The shifts might be sharper but it seems an incremental change in a car that’s all about taking massive strides. Give it more snap, more aggression and more speed please, Bentley.
Such is the level of grip and the increase in cornering speeds there’s no question the lack of hybrid boost does make itself known out in traction zones. In an ideal world some shorter ratios would just create a bit more fizz. Plus, that rear e-LSD can’t quite take the heat for fast and/or sideways track driving.
![Bentley Supersports](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/styles/media_embed/public/2026/08/DSC05527.jpg?itok=RHzIJX7N) 
Bentley assures us the software on this prototype was just a bit conservative, so let’s hope the finished cars don’t have the same habit of opening the diff quite so readily. Nobody wants a one tyre fire in their £343,900 Bentley Supersports. Mortifying. Yet for all this and the seemingly contradictory concept of a luxury GT stripped out sports car, I really enjoyed the Supersports.
Quite unexpectedly, it knows exactly what it is. A Bentley above all else, but with the recipe tweaked to give it a much more intense spice. It manages to exaggerate all the good stuff, uncover some hidden agility and locked down control but always remain true to Bentley’s core values.
It’s a car you want to use and enjoy, a car that makes you feel good about the world and a car that offers a blend of qualities you won’t find anywhere else. From the moment you shut the door, all your troubles melt away. I bet Travis Pastrana emerged without a single ache or pain. Well, a few less, anyway.
![](https://www.topgear.com/sites/default/files/news-listicle/image/2026/05/1-BMW-iX3-review-2026-UK.jpg?w=405&h=228)
summary: The new Bentley Supersports represents a dramatic departure for the brand by shedding over 500kg, removing the hybrid system, and converting to rear-wheel drive. Weighing just under 2,000kg, it is the lightest Bentley in 85 years, producing 657bhp and featuring extensive aerodynamic carbon-fibre upgrades. While it adopts a more track-focused, Porsche-influenced attitude with sharp handling and 300kg of downforce, it retains Bentley's signature opulent luxury interior.
key_points: The Bentley Supersports drops over 500kg of mass by removing the hybrid system, adopting rear-wheel drive, and utilizing extensive carbon fibre.
It is the lightest Bentley in 85 years at just under 2,000kg, powered by a 4.0-litre twin-turbocharged V8 producing 657bhp.
Only 500 units will be made, with prices starting from £343,900.
The car features aerodynamic upgrades like a carbon fibre roof and rear spoiler, generating 300kg of downforce and achieving up to 1.3g of lateral load on optional Trofeo RS tyres.

title: AI trial aims to detect depression in new mothers
author: Liz Johnson; Miya Chahal
content:
![Woman using a phone in front of a baby in a cot](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/9641/live/02b81e50-9bb6-11f1-ae8a-8d57110c5ba6.jpg)
The technology uses women's speech and facial expressions to determine their mood
- Published
A medical study is testing whether Artificial Intelligence (AI) could be used to detect depression in pregnant women or those who have recently given birth.
Researchers from the University of Nottingham and Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust have worked with AI firm BlueSky to develop an app that tracks participants' mood and behaviour.
The app works by asking users to complete tasks while software analyses their facial expressions, speech and automatic movements.
After finishing the task, the technology flags if patients are getting above a certain depression score. Researchers hope it will help women speak to their GP about mood changes during and after pregnancy.
The study, which started in 2024, is now in its final stages and researchers are aiming to finish in October.
A report by the University of Oxford, external last year found that in the UK, 39% of maternal deaths between six weeks and one year after pregnancy are suicides.
Dr Neil Nixon, one of the leading researchers on the project, said: "One thing we should remember is that suicide remains a really important cause of mortality in women in the post-natal period.
"Being able to identify clinical problems early on, at a point where we can intervene for those women, could really make a big difference."
The tasks vary from reading a few paragraphs of a novel to journalling their mood.
Nixon said that so far, about a third of women who have been through the study have been flagged for depression.
"The worry is that women don't realise their mood is changing. This software could change that," he said.
![Dr Neil Nixon standing in front of a bookshelf](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/960/cpsprodpb/8b35/live/83805ee0-97e1-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
Dr Neil Nixon is one of the leading researchers on the project
Lizzie, a mum from Long Eaton who took part in the trial, has two children and used the app when her youngest child was seven months.
She said people underestimate how hard it can be once you leave the hospital.
"You are so obsessed with the pregnancy, and you have so much support through the birth... and then you are just at home.
"That's when it really can be tricky.
"It's not all rainbows and butterflies. It's a really difficult time mentally for you, your identity and your mental health."
Sally Bunkman. from the charity PANDAS, which helps women suffering with perinatal mental illness, added: "People that use our services are often dismissed when they see a healthcare professional - they are told it's just the 'baby blues'.
"This technology has lots of potential and could empower women to talk more openly about their feelings to a doctor.
"But, women need to get support from an actual human - we don't want women being supported by an AI. We need human to human support. That is crucial."
Nixon said the technology will not be used to diagnose conditions, but instead support clinicians in their work.
He added: "We hope this will help women check in with their feelings at a time that is so important in their lives."
If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this article, support is available via the BBC Action Line
Listen to BBC Radio Nottingham on Sounds and follow BBC Nottingham on Facebook, external, on X, external, or on Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to eastmidsnews@bbc.co.uk, external or via WhatsApp, external on 0808 100 2210.
summary: A medical study is testing a new AI-powered app designed to detect depression in pregnant women and new mothers by analyzing their facial expressions, speech, and movements during tasks. Developed by researchers from the University of Nottingham, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, and AI firm BlueSky, the tool aims to help women identify changing moods and speak with their GPs early. Researchers emphasize that the technology is intended to support clinicians rather than diagnose conditions, while charities stress the ongoing necessity of human support.
key_points: Researchers from the University of Nottingham, Nottinghamshire Healthcare NHS Foundation Trust, and BlueSky developed an app to track mood and behavior using AI.
The app analyzes facial expressions, speech, and automatic movements as users complete tasks like reading or journalling.
The study, which began in 2024, is in its final stages and aims to conclude in October.
Developers state the technology is designed to support clinicians and help women discuss mood changes with their GP, rather than provide a medical diagnosis.
Charity representatives note the potential for the app to empower women, while stressing that actual human support remains crucial.

title: Fairphone 6+ review: the most repairable, ethical phone gets faster
author: Samuel Gibbs
content:
Fairphone’s top Android for 2026 is a little faster with more memory while maintaining full compatibility with its previous phone, including its repairable and ethical chops.
The Fairphone 6+ continues the Dutch cooperative’s mission to make consumer electronics longer lasting and more sustainable, containing 51% either recycled or ethically sourced materials while being fully repairable at home with just the one screwdriver included in the box.
It is also the first model to expand beyond Europe, going on sale in the US directly from Fairphone. But the new Android costs £70 (€50) more than the launch price of its predecessor, available from £569 (€649/$650), competing directly with Google’s £499 Pixel 10a and Apple’s £599 iPhone 17e.
![The back of the cobalt blue Fairphone 6+ stood up on a wooden table.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/e57377a18d0feeac30977f68cc125f4c0c1337c0/1309_800_4663_3730/master/4663.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The 6+ is an almost exact clone of the Fairphone 6, with the same plastic body, 120Hz OLED screen and fingerprint scanner in the power button. It also supports the same excellent modular accessories that simply screw into the back of the phone to add a lanyard, handle or wallet.
The new model is 2g heavier, but the biggest difference for the 6+ is an upgraded chip to the newer Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 and an additional 4GB of memory for 12GB in total.
The Gen 4 chip is about six to 10% faster in testing, which places it firmly in the mid-range category alongside the likes of the Nothing Phone 4a Pro with the same chip. It won’t win any performance awards and is significantly slower than chips used in Apple, Samsung or Google’s latest smartphones, but it feels snappy enough in use and can be used for light gaming without issue.
The battery life is very similar to the phone’s predecessor, lasting about a day and a half between charges with the screen actively used for about five hours across 5G and wifi, for messaging, note-taking, photos and browsing. Most will need to charge it nightly, which is a bit behind the curve. A full charge takes about 80 minutes using a 30W power adaptor (not included), hitting 50% in under half an hour.
![The camera app on the Fairphone 6+.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/25137389de60615beaeaca7fd0ecaa7c1c5abb9d/1329_803_3735_2988/master/3735.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The 6+ also has the same dual-camera system as its predecessor with a 50-megapixel main and 13MP ultra-wide camera. It has improved since its debut last year through software updates, which have fixed a few of the issues and inconsistencies. It can shoot pretty good photos with a bit of work and manages a reasonable 2x zoom. It isn’t the best in lower light conditions, though its new Super Night AI feature helps.
Specifications
- 
  Screen: 6.31in 120Hz FHD+ OLED (431ppi)
- 
  Processor: Qualcomm Snapdragon 7s Gen 4
- 
  RAM: 12GB
- 
  Storage: 256GB + microSD
- 
  Operating system: Android 16
- 
  Camera: 50MP + 13MP, 32MP selfie
- 
  Connectivity: 5G, eSIM, wifi 6E, NFC, Bluetooth 5.4 and GNSS
- 
  Water resistance: IP55 (splash/rain)
- 
  Dimensions: 156.6 x 73.3 x 9.6mm
- 
  Weight: 193g
Google’s Android 16 or e/OS
![The Moments interface on the Fairphone 6+.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/7d64735cb7a003c3aa70931006c27251a960fbc5/1310_677_4387_3510/master/4387.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The 6+ ships with last year’s Android 16, not the latest Android 17, but will be supported with updates until 2033 at least, which is roughly the same as mainstream rivals.
Fairphone’s software is generally clean and uncluttered with only an additional gallery app and the My Fairphone app for repair and diagnostics from the standard Android app loadout. It has Google’s Gemini in various bits, but no other AI additions to get in the way. It also features Fairphone’s “Moments” minimalist interface, activated by the big yellow switch on the side, for a less distracting smartphone experience.
But for those who want an alternative to Google’s Android, the phone is available with the privacy-focused, open-source version of Android, without Google services, called /e/OS.
Sustainability
![The power button and Moments switch of the Fairphone 6+.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/a4fbc65219069092ab54d5e884f5ead2e9c92593/818_457_5261_4209/master/5261.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
The battery will maintain at least 80% of its original capacity for 1,000 full charge cycles and it can be replaced at home using a single screwdriver along with the rest of the 12 modular components. Batteries cost £34.20, screens £77.00 and the main camera £59.88. The phone was awarded 10 out of 10 for repairability by specialists iFixit.
The handset is made with 51% recycled or fair materials, while Fairphone publishes life cycle reports for its products.
Price
The Fairphone Gen 6+ costs £569 (€649/$649.99) with Google Android or £598.63 (€699.99/$699.99) with e/OS.
For comparison, the Google Pixel 10a costs £499, the Apple iPhone 17e costs £599 and the Nothing Phone 4a Pro costs £519.
Verdict
The Fairphone 6+ continues to demonstrate that good, solid Android phones can be made fully repairable at home without specialist tools.
It is only a small spec bump on the original Fairphone 6, which helps keep up with mainstream rivals without sacrificing parts compatibility, sustainability or ethical credentials. It is also available directly in the US for the first time. But that also means the 6+ shares the same flaws as its predecessor.
The camera, battery life, performance and screen are all decent, if far from the best you can get for the money. However, those looking for a high-end smartphone experience best look elsewhere as the Fairphone can’t match a recent iPhone, Pixel or Galaxy S with similar levels of software support.
That makes it hard to recommend to everyone. But for those who prioritise repairability and ethical ethos, this is the phone for you.
 Pros: choice of Android operating systems, modular accessories, repairable-at-home design, recycled and fair materials, microSD card slot, good screen, five-year warranty, software support to 2033
Cons: mid-range performance, average battery life, fingerprint scanner can be tricky to press, average camera, cannot be submerged in water, no Android 17 yet.
summary: The Fairphone 6+ is an ethical, highly repairable Android smartphone that features a slight performance upgrade using the Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 chip and 12GB of RAM. It maintains full compatibility with previous modular accessories while expanding its direct sales market to the US for the first time. Although its camera, battery life, and mid-range performance lag behind mainstream competitors, it remains unmatched in sustainability and home-repair capability.
key_points: The Fairphone 6+ is made from 51% recycled or ethically sourced materials and achieved a 10 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit.
It upgrades to a Snapdragon 7s Gen 4 processor and 12GB of RAM, offering mid-range performance that is 6% to 10% faster than its predecessor.
The phone starts at £569 (€649/$649.99) and is the first Fairphone model to go on sale directly in the US.
It features a modular design that allows users to replace components like the battery and screen at home using a single screwdriver.
Software support is guaranteed until at least 2033, and buyers can choose between standard Android or the privacy-focused /e/OS.

title: In the wild: Shimano Dura-Ace R9300 groupset at La Vuelta
author: Dave Rome
content:
It’s no big secret that component manufacturers are always working on the next new thing. Like new phone releases, you used to be able to set your watch to new groupset releases. However, Shimano hasn’t offered that frequency in a while.
It’s been five years since we had the release of the current Dura-Ace R9200 generation, and whispers of a new Dura-Ace R9300 groupset have already been circling for a couple of years. Shimano themselves added fuel to the rumour fire with the recent release of the new Dura-Ace R9300 wheels, and multiple sightings of what’s assumed to be a matching generation of new pedal.
And yet, all our sources in the know have been telling us that new groupsets aren’t happening this year. So fancy our surprise when new Dura-Ace components broke cover at the Vuelta a España.
Let’s talk about what was captured outside the team bus prior to Stage 1.
What the photos tell
The sighting reveals, or at least confirms, a few things many have already assumed for the next generation of Shimano’s flagship group. Namely, it’s 13-speed, and there's still a version with a front derailleur.
The unexpected parts are the wires still connecting the derailleurs to what’s likely a central battery – just like current R9200/R8100/R7100 groupsets. Those aware of Shimano’s move to wireless shifting in mountain biking would have rightfully expected similar for the road, but it’s clear that the far smaller form factor of the photographed derailleur doesn’t allow space for onboard batteries.
![](https://escapecollective.com/content/images/thumbnail/Shimano-XTR-Di2-M9200-Drivetrain-Review-Escape-Collective-Dave-Rome-31-86a7f07f-4c43-4e2f-8290-0fd86100b086.jpg)
![](https://escapecollective.com/content/images/2026/08/New-Shimano-Dura-Ace-R9300-Vuelta-Espana-2026-Escape-Collective--2.jpg)
While what we see here could be an early prototype, the continued use of Shimano’s semi-wireless system (wireless shifters, wired derailleurs) aligns to rumours we’d previously heard.
Did we do a good job with this story?
summary: New Shimano Dura-Ace R9300 components have unexpectedly appeared at the Vuelta a España, contradicting sources that claimed no new groupsets would release this year. Photographs from the event confirm that the upcoming flagship groupset is 13-speed and retains a version with a front derailleur. Despite expectations of a fully wireless road setup, the new derailleurs still use wires connecting to a central battery due to their small form factor.
key_points: New Shimano Dura-Ace R9300 components were spotted at the Vuelta a España.
The upcoming flagship groupset features a 13-speed setup.
A version of the groupset with a front derailleur is confirmed to exist.
The derailleurs still use wires to connect to a central battery instead of being fully wireless.

title: PSA: Modern Warfare 4's Switch 2 Retail Version Is Apparently A Code-In-A-Box
author: Nintendo Life; Liam Doolan
content:
![Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4](https://images.nintendolife.com/2c136ad24abea/call-of-duty-modern-warfare-4.900x.jpg)
If you're wondering how exactly Activision will distribute the retail version of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on the Switch 2, some new information has surfaced via social media.
This update comes from Video Games Plus. According to the North American physical video game distributor, the Switch 2 version of MW4 will be a "code-in-box" release when it arrives this October. As it's "just a box with a download code inside", VGP says it won't be carrying the product.
This might not be the most surprising news if you're familiar with how the series operates nowadays, but it's still caused some upset online. Activision's file sizes, downloads and updates for the blockbuster titles have continued to rise, and existing releases have been managed through a dedicated game launcher, where you select what games, modes and content to install.
There's no official update about how exactly the installation for the Switch 2 version of the game will work, but this will be the first Call of Duty on a Nintendo platform in 13 years, so any file management will focus exclusively on this title. In early access on Switch 2, players simply download and launch the beta to play it.
When Switch 2 players join the fight this October, they can jump into the campaign and multiplayer modes. The multiplayer will also receive regular game updates. If there are any significant updates about the retail version of Call of Duty, we'll provide an update.
summary: According to North American distributor Video Games Plus, the physical retail version of Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 for the Switch 2 will be a code-in-a-box release containing only a download code. Because of this format, VGP has announced it will not carry the product. The game is scheduled to launch this October, marking the first Call of Duty title on a Nintendo platform in 13 years.
key_points: The Switch 2 retail version of Modern Warfare 4 is reportedly a code-in-a-box release.
Video Games Plus refused to carry the physical product due to it lacking a game card.
The game is set to launch this October with campaign and multiplayer modes.
This release marks the first Call of Duty title on a Nintendo platform in 13 years.

title: Weekly poll results: a clear favorite emerges from the Google Pixel 11 family
author: Peter
content:
Last week, we asked you which Pixel 11 model you would buy and now the results are in. The sentiment is trending towards negative with price being a common reason for skipping the 11 series.
Looking at the overall poll, many just aren’t interested in any Pixel 11 model. But those that do want one are mostly leaning towards the Pixel 11 Pro – it almost got more votes than the vanilla and the Pro XL models put together. Almost. The Pro XL is a distant second, while the pricey foldable barely got any love.
Focusing in on the Google Pixel 11 Pro, it received the biggest proportion of positive votes with 1 in 5 voters looking to buy one. Price is the biggest concern, but quite a few people are holding off until the reviews come in before making up their minds.
The larger Google Pixel 11 Pro XL is well liked too. Price remains a primary concern, so some will bide their time until the right deal comes along.
The vanilla Google Pixel 11 may have ranked #3 in the overall poll, but its individual poll shows that there is hope – a bigger proportion of voters is interested in buying one outright than the Pro XL. Also, more people may be swayed by reviews. Still, even though this is the cheapest Pixel 11 model (until the 11a launches), many consider it too expensive.
Last and clearly least, the Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold didn’t generate much interest – even with glowing reviews, we expect that Google will have trouble selling these. Part of this is easy enough to explain – some people just don’t like foldables, period. Them aside, quite a few voters don’t like this particular foldable and would rather get one from a different brand. Better pricing might help, but even then the future isn’t bright for the new Pro Fold.
We are working on testing the new Pixel 11 models, so stay tuned for our findings. If they prove to be meaningfully better than their Pixel 10 counterparts, then maybe some models will become more popular.
