title: iPhone 18 Pro Release Date Has Already Crushed The Competition
author: Ewan Spence
content:
Update, Sunday August 23: This article has been updated with details on the iPhone 18 Pro pricing and the precedent set by competing Android handsets.
Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro family on Wednesday, Sept. 9. Give or take a few days, this is the predictable launch window of every new iPhone. It’s also a date that allows Apple to be aggressive; the competition knows the date, knows what’s coming down the line, and is forced to avoid it as best they can. Apple’s preferred iPhone launch date is one of the most aggressive moves that the Cupertino business makes each year.
The iPhone 18 Pro And The Mid-Range Squeeze At IFA Berlin
Apple’s early-September iPhone 18 Pro launch systematically deprives IFA Berlin exhibitors of media oxygen, while mid-range Android devices face severe component margin pressure.
This year, IFA Berlin takes place from Sept. 4 to Sept. 8. Since 2005, it has taken place annually and is seen by many smartphone manufacturers as an opportunity to launch new hardware, akin to an “end-of-year Mobile World Congress.” While IFA is not exclusively for smartphones, it has seen key launch events in recent years, such as last year’s Galaxy S25 FE.
It’s not the best venue for launching premium handsets, even with the world’s press in attendance. The portfolio of new launches benefits mid-range handsets more than the flagships. That may offer IFA a slight advantage this year as Apple moves the vanilla iPhone 18 to spring 2027, putting similar pressure on MWC. Yet mid-range handsets are under the most financial pressure due to rising prices and lower stock levels of memory and storage across the production chain, making them a bet with far less return now that Apple has moved into the premium space.
The iPhone 18 Pro Has The Last-Mover Advantage Over Premium Android Phones
Samsung and Google are forced to compress their hardware release cycles to avoid direct marketing collisions with Apple’s dominant fourth-quarter iPhone timetable.
Apple has effectively secured a last-mover advantage in the premium space. Samsung has repeatedly delayed the launch of the Galaxy Z Foldable range to give it as much time as possible to become established before the iPhone arrives. Google has a similar choice to make on the Pixel, with just two weeks between the reviews of the Pixel 11 Pro arriving and the reveal of the iPhone 18 Pro to the world’s press; a moment that will hand Apple all the digital headlines and column inches it can handle.
Whether competing smartphones choose to avoid the iPhone and move further away from the commercially rich fourth quarter, or launch closer to and accept any momentum is going to be squashed once Apple’s smartphone neuters their efforts, the true winner is Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro can clear the bases when it launches, allowing incoming CEO John Ternus to start out with a continuity product which will dominate retail shelves.
The Android Competition Insulates The iPhone 18 Pro Price Rise
Update, Sunday August 23: This article has been updated with details on the iPhone 18 Pro pricing and the precedent set by competing Android handsets.
As Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reports, Apple is expected to increase the price of the iPhone 18 Pro between $100 and $200:
Two months ago, Apple boosted prices on nearly every major product category outside the iPhone, with affected Macs and iPads rising about 23% on average. The MacBook Air went up $200, the Mac Studio price jumped $500, and the iPad Air hike was $150. With the same memory and silicon shortages weighing on the iPhone, an increase there remains inevitable."
Although there will be sticker shock for consumers buying a new iPhone 18 Pro, it won't be as painful as you might think. The reason is another last-mover advantage the iPhone 18 Pro family has earned. Thanks to their summer product launches, both Samsung and Google have raised prices on their base smartphone models, largely due to the ongoing crunch in memory and storage chips. For months, consumers have been hearing stories of rising prices and have now faced them in retail stores and shopping sites.
Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max will be more expensive year-on-year compared to the iPhone 17 family, but consumers will see Apple simply ‘following the market conditions’ with the price rise, rather than being the first to ask for more money. The Galaxy and the Pixel took the pain so the iPhone will enjoy the gain.
iPhone 18 Pro Carrier Subsidies And Retail Dominance
North American carrier upgrade cycles align directly with Apple's September retail calendar, starving competing Android flagships of carrier marketing support.
Apple’s release of the iPhone, particularly in North America, sweeps away the competition on so many levels. It smothers other launch events and PR activities as it launches its own phone. With notable traffic boosts over the Android competition guaranteeing more digital inches and headlines, the associated media coverage drowns out alternatives.
With so many consumers locked into 12- or 24-month smartphone contracts that end just as the next iPhone hits retail shelves, carriers’ PR campaigns around the iPhone help bring customers back for another contract.
The Fixed iPhone 18 Pro Calendar Is An Unmatched Moat
Apple is locked into an early September release date for many reasons. Even knowing that, the competition has not found a simple way to match the elephant in the room. Apple will quite happily take advantage of this fixed launch date and the pressure it can apply to the wider smartphone ecosystem. The launch date of the iPhone 18 Pro remains a red-letter day for the industry.
summary: Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro family around September 9, capitalizing on a predictable release schedule that pressures competitors. The timing allows Apple to dominate media coverage, overshadow events like IFA Berlin, and secure a last-mover advantage over premium Android devices. Additionally, prior price hikes by competitors like Samsung and Google help insulate Apple from consumer backlash regarding anticipated $100 to $200 price increases.
key_points: Apple's predictable early-September launch window for the iPhone 18 Pro forces competitors to adjust their release schedules and deprives events like IFA Berlin of media attention.
Rival manufacturers such as Samsung and Google have compressed their hardware release cycles and raised their base prices due to memory and storage shortages.
Competitors taking the initial heat for higher prices allows Apple to increase the iPhone 18 Pro price by $100 to $200 without facing the worst of consumer sticker shock.
North American carrier upgrade cycles align with Apple's September release, driving customers back into contracts and starving competing Android flagships of marketing support.

title: Garmin teases August global release for new rugged smartwatches with seawater resistance
author: Alex Alderson
content:
Garmin has finally started hinting about the release of new smartwatches. For context, the Enduro 4, Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro have all appeared in leaks within the last few weeks. While the company has not addressed these directly, it has now confirmed the date of its next livestream.
As the video below shows, Garmin will host a ‘Play Harder’ livestream on August 25. Specifically, the event will commence at 11:00 UTC, albeit without a fixed runtime. However, if the launch of the Fenix 8 Pro is anything to go by (curr. $949 on Amazon), then next week’s livestream may only last 15 minutes or so.
![A brighter version of Garmin's 'Play Harder' teaser.](https://www.notebookcheck.net/fileadmin/_processed_/9/a/csm_garmin-fenix-9-official-teaser-mid_684e733e22.jpg)
At this stage, Garmin is giving nothing away about what it plans to unveil on August 25. Instead, it merely shows a surfer wearing some kind of wearable capable of withstanding extended exposure to seawater. Hence, we would expect the company to announce something with superior water resistance than recent Forerunner models like the Forerunner 570 or Forerunner 970. In that sense, a new Fenix or Enduro seems more probable at this stage.
In the meantime, a Czech retailer has been spotted listing the Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro ahead of schedule. Incidentally, SkiAndBike have not mentioned the Enduro 4 or a new Fenix E yet. Please see our corresponding article for more details and Fenix 9 series pricing expectations.
summary: Garmin has confirmed it will host a 'Play Harder' livestream event on August 25 at 11:00 UTC. Although the company has not explicitly named the upcoming devices, a teaser featuring a surfer wearing a seawater-resistant wearable strongly suggests the launch of new rugged smartwatches, such as the Fenix or Enduro series. Meanwhile, leaks have already surfaced, including early listings for the Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro by a Czech retailer.
key_points: Garmin scheduled a 'Play Harder' livestream event for August 25 at 11:00 UTC.
A teaser video hints at a new wearable with superior seawater resistance.
Expected announcements likely include new rugged models from the Fenix or Enduro series.
The Fenix 9 and Fenix 9 Pro have already been spotted in early retail listings ahead of the official reveal.

title: PS5's Best-Selling Games List Is Broken on the PS Store
author: Push Square; Sammy Barker
content:
![PS5's Best-Selling Games List Is Broken on the PS Store 1](https://images.pushsquare.com/eab08ed8515ac/ps5s-best-selling-games-list-is-broken-on-the-ps-store-1.900x.jpg)
Good news for the makers of 007 First Light and 1000xRESIST – both games are currently appearing on the PS Store homepage due to a glitch.
Sony usually shows the most popular games in each country across a variety of categories, ranging from pre-orders to downloads.
But these are currently ordered alphabetically, as opposed to by sales performance.
That means Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve has now “usurped” GTA 6 and Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 as PS5’s most wanted game, alongside quaint FMV effort Akiba Lost.
The bug is consistent across the console and web store, and it’s broken on the Browse tab too.
It’s a minor glitch so I’d expect this to be resolved relatively quickly, and the good news is this isn’t really a big problem. While not ideal, it’s only a tiny browsing inconvenience if you’re hitting up the PS Store right now.
As far as I can tell everything appears as it should through search, so I guess this is just an error pertaining to the ordering of the displayed games.
I’m going to go out on a limb and say even Sony will have this fixed in a few hours.
summary: The PS Store's best-selling games list is currently experiencing a glitch that orders games alphabetically rather than by sales performance. This bug affects both the console and web store interfaces, as well as the Browse tab. However, search functionality remains unaffected, and the minor browsing inconvenience is expected to be fixed quickly.
key_points: The PS Store's best-selling games list is currently ordered alphabetically instead of by sales.
The glitch affects both the console store and the web store, including the Browse tab.
Search functionality continues to work properly despite the display error.
The bug is a minor browsing inconvenience that is expected to be resolved quickly.

title: The new Halloween video game has been banned in Australia – and not because of the violence
author: Jackson Ryan
content:
Halloween’s Michael Myers is one of film’s most feared boogeymen, responsible for some of the most brutal on-screen deaths in horror cinema. The US video game developer Illfonic looked to reproduce those terrors in its upcoming title Halloween: The Game, with gruesome killings a major focus of the gameplay: for instance, you can stomp another player’s head through a toilet seat, or fry their brain by throwing them through a television screen.
But Australians will not be able to play Halloween, because it has been refused classification by the Australian Classification Board, which means it is banned from sale within the country. And it’s not because of the violence or murders.
In the game, players can smoke marijuana to see the location of Michael Myers in order to avoid being killed – a use of drugs that the Classification Board has deemed a “gameplay advantage”. Under the Guidelines for the Classification of Computer Games 2023, video games are refused classification if they contain “illicit or proscribed drug use related to incentives or rewards”.
“Halloween: The Game contains illicit drug use that is linked to an incentive or reward, in that use of the drug provides a gameplay advantage to the player. It is on this basis that the game has been refused classification, as required under the Code and Guidelines,” the board wrote in a recent statement.
In the wake of the decision, Illfonic’s social media accounts have been flooded with comments from irate Australians. An FoI officer said the Classification Board had received more than 500 complaints in relation to Halloween: The Game.
The uproar has resurfaced longstanding grievances about how games are classified in Australia compared with film and television, and the inability for adults to access games widely available in other parts of the world.
Claire Henry, an associate professor in screen at Flinders University and an Australian Research Council fellow, says the board enforced the guidelines correctly but the controversy around the decision highlights “a mismatch between the community standards and the classification standards”.
The decision on Halloween: The Game follows several high-profile cases that have resulted in games such as State of Decay, Wasteland 3 and Saints Row IV banned in Australia for the same reason: incentivised drug use. All of these games were later reclassified after censoring aspects of their gameplay.
![Saints Row IV still](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/c08f897ea7a85094ed9125bbd4242b37952a2592/148_0_4800_2880/master/4800.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Dan Golding, a professor of media at Monash University, says that two assumptions have been baked into the classifying of games in Australia. “Games have always been regulated based on the assumption there is something more impactful about doing, in a game, than there is about watching, in a film,” he says.
“A second assumption is that games are for kids – or at least the regulation system exists to protect kids.”
Ron Curry has battled these assumptions in skirmishes with the Classification Board over his nearly two decades as CEO of the Interactive Games and Entertainment Association (IGEA). Alongside a dogged public campaign and a cadre of journalists, the IGEA helped introduce an R18+ category for video games in 2013, the absence of which had stopped several games being released in Australia before.
After the R18+ classification was brought in, Curry noted the job was not finished – the trade-off for introducing the category was that video games were still seen as a distinct form of media, with greater risks attached.
“It still very clearly said games are different to all other media, it’s more dangerous, and we need to treat it more carefully,” Curry says.
after newsletter promotion
Interactivity – the doing Golding refers to – has always underlined this belief. The guidelines for games, introduced alongside the R18+ rating, state that “as a general rule computer games may have a higher impact than similarly themed depictions of the classifiable elements in film, and therefore greater potential for harm or detriment, particularly to minors”.
Curry points to the Australian government’s own research that has suggested interactivity may not increase the impact of video games, particularly in regards to violent content, and there has been limited research on interactivity around drug use, sex, gambling and nudity.
Margaret Anderson, a former director of the Classification Board, says the huge focus on interactivity in games drove her nuts during her seven years on the board. She points to decades of research showing games are predominantly played by adults.
“Can we stop pretending that the way we classify games in this country, in 2026, is appropriate for adults? Because it’s not,” Anderson says.
Academics have shown the current classification system isn’t just preventing access to games, however. Often, the standards are incoherent.
Marcus Carter, founder of the Sydney Games and Play Lab at the University of Sydney, recently led a study – yet to be peer reviewed – that showed inconsistencies across the classifications of mobile games in the Apple App Store and Google Play Store. In 18 separate cases across the 31 top-grossing mobile games, four different age ratings were included for a single game.
Carter describes the current system as “not fit for purpose”.
The worry, for experts like Carter and Henry, is that the inconsistent standards have a negative impact on how the community views classifications and age ratings.
“Inconsistencies can kind of undermine public confidence in the classification system,” says Henry. “It is a good system in many ways, and we’ve got to maintain that trust.”
The Australian government is undertaking a review of the classification guidelines with the aim of delivering a simpler, more consistent approach across films, games and publications. Among a raft of proposals – including introducing a PG13 rating and adjusting the MA15+ classification to MA16+ – one idea is to “remove the harsher judgement of video games’ interactivity”. IGEA and Henry have made submissions to the review.
In a statement to the Guardian, a spokesperson from the Department of Infrastructure, Transport, Regional Development, Communications, Sport and the Arts said: “The Australian Government is working to modernise the National Classification Scheme to ensure it remains aligned with community standards and helps Australians make informed decisions about what they read, watch and play. This work is ongoing.”
Illfonic has shown no sign it will censor Halloween: The Game and have its classification reviewed in Australia. Illfonic and the game’s co-publisher Gun Interactive did not respond to requests for comment.
Though the instances of Australia banning games have been rare occurrences, one future decision looms large: how will Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment in a franchise packed with sex, drugs and violence, be rated?
For Anderson, the way forward is simple.
“The foundational pillar of classification in Australia is that adults should be able to read, hear, see, play what they want,” she says. “Can we please respect that fact?”
summary: The upcoming video game Halloween: The Game has been banned in Australia after being refused classification by the Australian Classification Board. Rather than the game's brutal violence, the ban stems from a mechanic where players use marijuana to gain a gameplay advantage, which violates guidelines against incentivized illicit drug use. The decision has sparked public backlash and reignited criticism from experts regarding Australia's strict and often inconsistent video game classification standards.
key_points: Halloween: The Game was refused classification in Australia because players can use marijuana to gain a gameplay advantage, violating rules against incentivized illicit drug use.
The ban generated hundreds of complaints and renewed longstanding debates over Australia's video game classification system and its treatment of interactivity compared to film.
Similar bans for incentivized drug use have previously affected games like State of Decay, Wasteland 3, and Saints Row IV, though those titles were later reclassified after censorship.
Experts and academics argue that current classification standards are outdated, incoherent, and fail to reflect community standards for adult gamers.

title: Amazon Hikes Prices by as Much as 60% Across Echo, Fire TV, Kindle Lines
author: Will McCurdy
content:
![](https://sm.pcmag.com/t/pcmag_uk/news/a/amazon-hik/amazon-hikes-prices-by-as-much-as-60-across-echo-fire-tv-kin_wge7.1920.jpg) (Credit: Will Greenwald)
2026 has been a traumatic year for cash-strapped consumer technology lovers so far, with major players like Apple, Dell, HP and Asus all hiking prices. And it doesn't look like the second half is shaping up to be much better.
Amazon has now hiked prices across a range of its smart home devices, as well as its Kindle line, and its Fire TV stock by as much as 60%, citing the ongoing chip crisis and component inflation. Its cheaper items appear to have been the most impacted by price rises, first spotted by Fortune.
Echo Dot is set to jump $30—60%—from $49.99 to $79.99, while the Echo Show 11 will jump $30 from $219.99 to $249.99.
Meanwhile the 16-gigabyte Kindle will go from $109.99 to $149.99, while its 16-gigabyte Kindle Paperwhite will go from $159.99 to $199.99. Amazon's Fire TV Stick HD will rise about 14% from $34.99 to $39.99, while the Fire TV Stick 4K Max rose $25 (over 40%) from $59.99 to $84.99. Amazon's wireless mesh networking system, the eero 7, was one of the least impacted products, rising 14.30% from $349.99 to $399.99. Meanwhile, the eero Pro 7 also rose 14.30% from $699.99 to $799.99.
One of the only product lines spared was Amazon's Ring series, which saw no price rises.
An Amazon spokeswoman attributed the company’s decision to “significant increases in memory and storage component costs.” She added: “After absorbing these increases for as long as we could, we recently adjusted pricing across our product lines.”
Amazon's prices might no longer look so appealing, but many of its competitors have also bumped prices in recent months. Fire Stick competitor Roku bumped the prices of its Roku Ultra streaming device $50, from $100 to $150. Meanwhile, its entry-level Roku Streaming Stick moved to $40 from $30.
The Echo Dot is still cheaper than Google's Google Home Speaker, which retails at $99.99, though the price gap has thinned significantly.
summary: Amazon has increased prices by up to 60% across its Echo, Fire TV, Kindle, and eero product lines, citing rising memory and storage component costs and an ongoing chip crisis. Cheaper items were impacted the most by the price hikes, while the Ring series was one of the few product lines spared. Competitors such as Apple, Dell, HP, Asus, and Roku have also recently raised their prices.
key_points: Amazon increased prices across various devices by as much as 60%.
The price hikes affect Echo smart home devices, Kindle e-readers, Fire TV stock, and eero networking systems.
Cheaper items, such as the Echo Dot, experienced the highest percentage increases.
Amazon attributed the price adjustments to significant increases in memory and storage component costs.
Competitors like Roku have also raised prices on their streaming devices.

title: The ‘GTA 6’ Leaks Get Higher Quality With No End In Sight
author: Paul Tassi
content:
We are approaching a week of non-stop Grand Theft Auto 6 leaks from a so-far unstoppable leaker, Cyberleeks, who appears to have a full build of the game. Or at least an old one. They are not taking weekends off, and there have been a number of leaks since the last update, each one getting higher in quality than the last and we are now far past the blurrier footage we began with. We are actually approaching the level of quality we could see in this upcoming week’s Netflix GTA 6 gameplay special.
Among the recent leaks over the past 48 hours or so:
- Cyberleeks released footage from inside a GTA 6 strip club, rewarding observers after they pumped up his crypto coin past a $3 million market cap. The footage is nothing especially scandalous, but using binoculars we get a look at the quality of some of the NPC models’ faces, which are quite good.
- A new clip has a car driving around with what appears to be gasoline in its bed, resulting in an instant death crash with some odd physics and sound effects (remember, none of these are finished builds and the game is still being polished as we speak ahead of release). This appears to be a reference to an actual real-life event that happened years ago where a video captured a man filling up the bed of his truck with gasoline.
- At one point, a specific clip is released in which Jason says he needs to “gotta take a leak.” Ha.
- The latest clip is a very high-quality piece of footage shot from an airplane, showing the Vice City skyline at night. Minus the watermarks, it seems like something that could be in an official gameplay reveal.
- One of the clips has a message for Jason to “return to Lucia,” the first reference to the other playable character in the game. Many wonder why there has been no footage of her yet, the theory being that Cyberleek is still early-ish in the game before she is actually playable.
- On top of this, a new poll on Cyberleek’s website is now taking votes on whether they release footage of the beach, a second strip club or a nudist town next.
The longest stretch of time without a Cyberleeks leak was about 24 hours, during which people believed they were caught, but that was not the case. Take-Two seems to have eased up on the whack-a-mole of DMCA takedowns on all these clips given how fast they are spreading (still, I would not post them, nor am I even linking to them here). They are busy subpoenaing everyone from Microsoft to Discord to now X in order to find specific account information, which even includes “fake” profiles for Cyberleek (who has said they have never had an X account).
This entire situation is teetering on a knife’s edge right now. So far, nothing Cyberleek has leaked has been some wild reveal about what’s coming, as wild as the situation itself may be. Rockstar wants absolutely none of this online, of course, but Cyberleeks has stopped short of outright story spoilers, though that could change any moment. We’ll see if there’s another leak by the time I’ve finished writing this article. As ever, Rockstar or Take-Two have made no public comment, nor have they responded to my requests.

title: Gurman: iPhone Ultra Wows Early Testers, Except for Its Camera
author: Tim Hardwick
content:
Apple's upcoming foldable iPhone Ultra is winning over the few people who have had hands-on time with the device, though the camera setup may leave some users wanting, according to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman.
![Apple Foldable Thumb](https://images.macrumors.com/t/WmYNENGA95YGRkAlvJXDrf2Vqko=/400x0/article-new/2025/08/Apple-Foldable-Thumb.jpg?lossy)
Writing in his latest Power On newsletter, Gurman says people who have used the device – which is reportedly referred to internally as the iPhone Ultra – like how it fits in your pocket, as well as the feel and durability of its hinge mechanism. Testers have also apparently praised the new iPad-like app layouts that take advantage of the larger internal display when the phone is unfolded.
Beyond productivity, video, and gaming, Gurman says Apple's foldable device also performs well as a camera viewfinder. However, the device lacks a telephoto lens, which could cost Apple some sales given the expected price. The device is expected to feature a dual-lens rear camera system built around a 48-megapixel main lens paired with an ultra-wide lens.
The foldable is also expected to fall back on Touch ID integrated into the side button instead of in-display Face ID – a compromise Apple has reportedly made to keep it around 4.5mm thick when unfolded. But like Gurman says, some users may prefer this traditional biometric setup. Like Samsung's recently released Z Fold 8, the iPhone Ultra is said have a 5.5-inch outer display and a roughly 7.8-inch inner display when opened, making for a wide book-style design.
Apple's first foldable is set to be unveiled alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max at a launch event on or around September 9. Reports suggest the device could start at $2,000 and even climb past $2,500 for higher storage tiers.
summary: According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, early testers are praising the upcoming foldable iPhone Ultra for its pocketability, durable hinge, and iPad-like app layouts. However, the device is expected to lack a telephoto lens, potentially hurting sales given its high anticipated price point. The foldable will reportedly feature a 4.5mm thickness when unfolded, side-mounted Touch ID, and screen sizes comparable to Samsung's Z Fold 8.
key_points: Early testers praise the iPhone Ultra's pocketability, durable hinge, and internal display app layouts.
The device features a dual-lens rear camera system but lacks a telephoto lens.
To maintain a 4.5mm unfolded thickness, the phone relies on side-button Touch ID instead of in-display Face ID.
The foldable is rumored to feature a 5.5-inch outer display and a roughly 7.8-inch inner display.
The device is expected to be unveiled on or around September 9, with prices starting between $2,000 and $2,500.

title: Xbox Now Has 88 Profile Badges, And Here's What They Mean
author: Pure Xbox; Fraser Gilbert
content:
![Xbox Now Has 88 Profile Badges, And Here's What They All Mean](https://images.purexbox.com/c903f2fc469f4/xbox-now-has-88-profile-badges-and-heres-what-they-all-mean.900x.jpg)
The folks over at Team Xbox have been making a quite a big deal of Profile Badges recently, adding new ways to view them in the latest Xbox Insider builds and even incorporating a new one for those who bought the Xbox One in 2013.
And to be honest, I've never personally paid that much attention to them until now, but a website known as "xct.live" does a nice job at not only highlighting all 88 of them, but also explaining what they mean and how rare they are.
Here's a look at the social media post that inspired this article, and then we'll break it down a bit:
Firstly, 15 out of the 88 Xbox Profile Badges are all about how much gamerscore you've earned over the years, ranging from 1,000 to 10 million. There are also 40 badges that are dedicated to how many years you've been part of Xbox Live, although many of these aren't yet achievable because Xbox hasn't even been around for 40 years!
In fact, the "40 years on Xbox Live badge" won't be obtainable until November 15th of 2042:
That leaves us with 33 more Xbox Profile Badges that all exist for different things. There are some that have been quite easily obtainable over the years, such as being part of Xbox Live Gold before it was removed, but many of the others are badges that were given to employees for working on certain projects such as consoles.
Here's an at-a-glance example of these from the website:
![Xbox Now Has 88 Profile Badges, And Here's What They All Mean 2](https://images.purexbox.com/d7bb66af5bb2d/xbox-now-has-88-profile-badges-and-heres-what-they-all-mean-2.900x.jpg)
Ultimately, there's no way of actually getting access to all 88 Xbox Profile Badges, and some of them have actually been retired in recent years, while others are just extremely rare (such as being part of the Xbox Live team in 2002!).
By all means go and have look at each of these in detail for yourself, and it's also worth noting that Xbox Fandom has a great list of most of the Xbox Profile Badges as well, including some extra clarification on what's been retired specifically. Let us know how many you've got down in the comments below!
summary: Team Xbox has drawn attention to the 88 profile badges available on the platform, which include milestones for gamerscore and years on Xbox Live, alongside special project badges for employees. While the website xct.live outlines what each badge means and its rarity, it is impossible for any single user to obtain all 88. Some of the badges are currently unachievable, such as the 40-year Xbox Live badge, while others have been retired or are extremely rare.
key_points: There are a total of 88 Xbox profile badges tracked by the website xct.live.
Fifteen badges are based on gamerscore earned, ranging from 1,000 to 10 million.
Forty badges are dedicated to years spent on Xbox Live, with the 40-year badge unattainable until November 2042.
Other badges include those for former Xbox Live Gold members and special project badges given to employees.
Certain badges are retired or extremely rare, making it impossible for any user to collect all 88.

title: Garmin Fenix 9 leaked by retailer ahead of upcoming Garmin event
author: Silvio Werner
content:
Rumors surrounding the new Fenix generation have circulated for weeks, pointing to an imminent release. A retailer leak reported by media outlets has now added weight to these expectations. Czech retailer skiandbike.cz briefly listed 18 separate Fenix 9 variants. The listings appear plausible overall; For instance, the 43 mm Garmin Fenix 9 AMOLED in Bare Titanium Fog was listed at a price equivalent to roughly €1,015 ($1,185).
The leaked listings cover the expected size options: 43 mm, 47 mm, and 51 mm. However, the Garmin Fenix 9 Pro was listed exclusively as a 51 mm and 47 mm variant, equipped with Garmin inReach technology for satellite connectivity. Integrated inReach functionality is not limited to the Pro model, as several standard 43 mm and 47 mm Fenix 9 AMOLED versions are also shown with satellite features. Additionally, a 47 mm Garmin Fenix 9 Pro Solar inReach Titanium model made an appearance. Neither a Fenix E 2, an Enduro 4, nor a MicroOLED variant has surfaced in these listings so far.
While retailer leaks should always be taken with a grain of salt, this inventory dump looks fundamentally solid. Garmin is widely expected to announce the new Fenix series on August 25 at 1:00 p.m. CET during its "Play Harder" livestream event.
summary: Czech retailer skiandbike.cz briefly leaked 18 variants of the upcoming Garmin Fenix 9, supporting rumors of an imminent release. The listings revealed various sizes, pricing details, and the inclusion of satellite connectivity through integrated inReach technology across multiple models. Garmin is widely expected to officially announce the new Fenix series during its August 25 livestream event.
key_points: Czech retailer skiandbike.cz listed 18 separate Garmin Fenix 9 variants ahead of an official announcement.
Leaked sizes include 43 mm, 47 mm, and 51 mm options, with specific pricing indicated for models like the 43 mm AMOLED in Bare Titanium Fog.
Integrated inReach satellite connectivity is featured on the Fenix 9 Pro as well as several standard 43 mm and 47 mm AMOLED versions.
Garmin is expected to formally unveil the new Fenix series on August 25 at 1:00 p.m. CET during its 'Play Harder' livestream event.

title: Going Platinum: I Only Played Sound Shapes Because I Wanted at Least One PS Vita Plat
author: Push Square; Stephen Tailby
content:
![Going Platinum: I Only Played Sound Shapes Because I Wanted at Least One PS Vita Plat 1](https://images.pushsquare.com/4431a045c6ab6/going-platinum-i-only-played-sound-shapes-because-i-wanted-at-least-one-ps-vita-plat-1.900x.jpg)
Platinum Trophy #34: Sound Shapes
Date Earned: 31st October 2021
Dopamine Index:
Hello! Been a minute since the last one of these, hasn't it? Sorry about that. I will be better, just as Kratos tells us.
Funnily enough, after the last Going Platinum, which was quite a personal and meaningful one for me, this edition is sort of the opposite.
I played Sound Shapes on PS Vita, and the primary motivation was, I'm afraid, Trophies. I simply wanted a PS Vita platinum, and this neat little game was what I chose.
I think this might be the most "Trophy hunter" I've ever been, just looking for another easy platinum to add to my collection.
That's not to say I didn't connect with the game, or enjoy it on its own merits; I definitely did. It's well worth playing if you haven't already.
Sound Shapes is a very simple game and very well-suited to the Vita, I think. It's essentially a 2D platformer set to music.
You control a little ball that can stick to objects in the environment, and you just hop over obstacles and hazards and soak in the music, and that's pretty much it.
Trophies are similarly straightforward; all you need to do to net the platinum is beat every level in the base game's campaign. Easy peasy, and it doesn't take long.
Through various DLC packs, there are a lot of other Trophies up for grabs, but they're not required for the top trinket.
I wish I had a bit more to say about the game itself, but to be honest I think I platinumed Sound Shapes in one or two sittings and moved on from it very quickly.
It deserves a bit more love than that. I really like the block colour visuals and simple geometry, and obviously the soundtrack is nice too, with numerous artists I recognise but frankly couldn't hum a single one of their songs.
It's good! And you should play it for more than the Trophies. Don't be like me.
Cheers, Sound Shapes.
Do you have the platinum Trophy for Sound Shapes? Tell us in the comments section below.
summary: The author played the 2D musical platformer Sound Shapes primarily to earn a platinum trophy on the PS Vita. Although driven by trophy hunting, the author found the game simple, enjoyable, and well-suited to the handheld console. The platinum trophy requires only beating the base game's campaign levels, which can be accomplished quickly.
key_points: The author's primary motivation for playing Sound Shapes was to earn a PS Vita platinum trophy.
Sound Shapes is a 2D platformer set to music where players control a ball navigating obstacles.
The platinum trophy is earned simply by beating every level in the base game's campaign.
The game features block color visuals, simple geometry, and a notable soundtrack.

title: Sony's PlayStation terms of service reminder email couldn't have landed at a worse time
author: Vikki Blake
content:
PlayStation users have received an unprompted reminder of exactly what they do and don't own on the platform, days before a planned boycott over Sony's decision to end new PlayStation discs from 2028.
"You recently accepted the following PlayStation terms (the "Terms"): PlayStation Terms of Service, PlayStation Code of Conduct, PlayStation End User License Agreement, PlayStation Privacy Policy," reads an email posted to Reddit on 18th August (thanks, Kotaku).
"For your convenience and future reference, we have included full copies of the Terms in this email. Please retain this email for your records."
Why i received an email from PlayStation that says „you recently accepted the following PlayStation terms […]“ although i didn‘t used my account for months?
by u/THE_NO_NAME_ONE in PlayStationSolutions
Several recipients said they'd received the email despite not touching their PS4 or PS5 in months. Rather than linking out to the full terms, the email reproduced each referenced document in full, including the section of the Software EULA covering digital purchases.
"The Software is licensed to you, not sold," it reads. "You are granted a limited, non-exclusive, non-transferable, and personal license to play or use the Software for your private, non-commercial use on the system or device it was intended for." The terms go on to restrict things like renting, modifying, or obtaining games through unauthorised means.
The email comes just as an attempted PlayStation boycott gets underway. Organised by fan group DoesItPlay, the #PSBlackout campaign runs from 23rd to 30th August and asks participants to log off, avoid purchases, and cancel subscriptions in protest at Sony's move away from physical media.
Sony was asked about its decision to kill off physical media in PlayStation's latest earnings call. The company, which announced that it will be ending the production and sale of discs for PlayStation games in early 2028, reaffirmed its stance on the matter, but noted that it understands why people have such strong feelings about the situation.
"There are various reasons we made this decision, the biggest being that the digitalisation of content overall has been progressing, that's the big factor," Sony chief financial officer Lin Tao said during a Q&A. "It's not just for PlayStation, but for all kinds of content; digitalisation is progressing."
summary: PlayStation users recently received unprompted emails containing full copies of Sony's terms of service, including clauses stating that digital software is licensed rather than sold. The timing coincided with an upcoming #PSBlackout boycott organized by fans protesting Sony's decision to phase out new PlayStation discs by 2028. Sony defended the shift away from physical media during an earnings call, citing the ongoing trend toward content digitalization.
key_points: Sony sent users an unprompted email containing full copies of the PlayStation terms of service and digital EULA.
The email explicitly reminded users that digital software is licensed to them rather than sold.
The email arrived just before the #PSBlackout campaign, a fan-organized boycott running from August 23 to 30.
The boycott was organized in protest of Sony's decision to end the production and sale of physical game discs in 2028.
Sony CFO Lin Tao defended the discontinuation of physical media, citing the industry-wide shift toward digital content.

title: I tested the viral Shark CryoGlow LED face mask 100 times – it’s not right for everyone
author: Sarah Matthews
content:
Of all the LED masks I’ve tested, the Shark CryoGlow feels like the most heavily marketed. Touted as a one-stop shop for anti-ageing, blemish-busting and undereye cooling, it’s trickled its way into countless influencer morning routines and post-work wind-downs, slowly but surely filling up my social media timeline.
As an acne-prone woman whose work life revolves around beauty tech, the adverts are well placed. But that doesn’t negate the fact that, to the average consumer, LED therapy still reeks of pseudoscience. If my younger self got wind that I was strapping a glowing mask to my face every day, she would die laughing.
Thankfully, I’ve spent months researching LED masks and have found that red-light therapy is backed by scientific research dating to the 1990s. This includes studies on skin rejuvenation, wound healing and anti-ageing.
I’ve had this mask for almost two years and have completed more than 100 light therapy treatments in that time. That makes this the most thoroughly tested product I’ve ever reviewed, and there’s a reason it became such a mainstay in my skincare routine. Here’s my full verdict on the CryoGlow, and why I’ve recently jumped ship in favour of a competitor.
How I tested
![The writer wearing a blue-glowing Shark CryoGlow seen in a mirror](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/d5ccddf4c8bd5e20a6485d1656b373697830d8a1/521_589_3043_2435/master/3043.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
I’ve tested 14 other options in my quest to find the best LED mask – which isn’t just about staring at your skin in the mirror and waiting for changes. For each LED mask I test, I consider how comfortable it is to wear for daily treatments, whether the eye guards block light effectively, as well as the number and brightness of the LEDs. I’m also looking for simple controls.
To test the mask’s effectiveness, I noted the appearance, feel and texture of my skin before and after two months of daily treatments. I tried all the settings, including the undereye cooling, for at least four nights each, then chose my favourite setting for the rest of the test.
What you need to know
![Closeup of the back Shark CryoGlow LED face mask and its controller unit.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/15f3b6865c43c2d21b753a9d7bdbc7be245cc2d0/615_0_2100_1680/master/2100.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Many will be familiar with Shark’s vacuum cleaners and hair care tools, but it hasn’t been in the skincare game for long. The 2024 CryoGlow was its first foray, followed by the 2025 FacialPro Glow, a hydro and temperature therapy tool. While the FacialPro Glow came with a laundry list of usage warnings and a high risk of user error, the CryoGlow’s LED therapy is far less likely to go wrong.
In LED therapy, each wavelength of light penetrates different levels of the skin, which can trigger specific natural processes. The CryoGlow has 160 LEDs that shine across three wavelengths: red light to help stimulate skin healing and collagen production; near-infrared light, which penetrates deeper into the skin; and blue light, which reduces acne-causing bacteria on the skin’s surface. It’s worth noting that blue light can cause hyperpigmentation on darker skin tones, so it should be used with caution.
The wavelengths are arranged into three pre-programmed LED settings, starting with a six-minute anti-ageing setting, which combines red and near-infrared light. The Blemish Repair mode takes eight minutes and begins with blue and near-infrared light, followed by red light, which Shark says helps heal breakouts faster. After six to eight treatments, Shark recommends continuing with Skin Sustain, which combines all the light types at once in a four-minute treatment.
The CryoGlow is also the only LED mask to have cooling pads under the eyes, which help to depuff the area. Cooling treatments alone can last from five to 15 minutes or can be used alongside the LED treatments. In each case, there are three temperature levels.
The mask costs £299.99 at full price (from £245.32 at the time of writing), which puts it firmly in the middle of the LED mask market. Cheaper masks, such as the £119 Silk’n 100, offer a range of colours, but no infrared and tend not to be arranged into preset treatments, or have any extras such as undereye cooling. Conversely, more expensive masks can have brighter lights and deeper-penetrating near-infrared lights. The £499.99 CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy mask is a fantastic example of this.
Shark CryoGlow specifications
Price: £299.99
Recommended use: one treatment daily
Settings: Better Ageing, Blemish Repair, Skin Sustain, undereye cooling 
Treatment time: four to eight minutes (LED), or five to 15 minutes (cooling)
Suitable for: all skin types (excluding certain skin conditions); darker skin tones should use caution with Blemish Repair mode 
Battery life: seven to 17 treatments, depending on cooling pad use
Charging time: three hours
Contents: Shark CryoGlow mask, clip-on undereye adjusters, USB-C charging cable and plug
What we love
![Shark CryoGlow LED face mask on a wooden tabletop.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/49c5d74de7ce94916a22b1710df96f9183c0f526/408_0_2100_1680/master/2100.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
As an acne-prone person, I benefited most from the Blemish Repair mode. Unlike cheaper masks, which use blue light alone, the preset treatment combining blue and red light may be more effective at treating acne, and I’ve found that to be true in my tests. The red light offers a gentler treatment because it helps promote wound healing and calm inflammation, reducing the appearance of post-acne red marks. It’s far more convenient to have this as a preset treatment than to keep switching between different colours. After eight weeks of treatments, I noticed far fewer breakouts, and any that did pop up healed far quicker – a few days rather than a week without the treatment.
After eight weeks, as Shark recommends, I switched to using the four-minute Skin Sustain mode. That treatment did exactly what it said: maintain my calm, clear skin until the next hormonal breakout reared its head. Thankfully, it was easy to switch back to the blemish treatment on those occasions.
In my week testing the Better Ageing setting, I noticed my skin was more even, with less pigmentation. And while I don’t always get puffy undereyes, I enjoyed using the cooling pads during hay fever season. It’s not a cure for hay fever, but a quick cooling session soothed the area and left it feeling far more comfortable. While I could get similar results from a cold compress stored in the fridge, the electric Peltier coolers meant the pads stayed cold for the duration, rather than warming up on contact with the skin.
That said, using the cooling pads drained the battery far faster than when they weren’t being used. When I tested the battery life using LED therapy alone, I was able to complete 17 treatments before the mask needed recharging. But when I switched the cooling on to full whack, the mask conked out after seven. That’s a dramatic drop-off. Most LED masks I’ve tested have run out of charge after about 10 days, though, so I think weekly charging is reasonable considering the cooling power on offer.
after newsletter promotion
For safety, the mask dims when removed from the face, and proximity sensors brighten the lights as soon as the mask is on your face. When the mask is fitted correctly, the eyes are well shielded from the light.
Thanks to its sturdy plastic build, the mask weighs 537g, which means it’s heavier than flexible silicone masks. To combat this, there is comfortable padding at the forehead, nose and brow bone, which is where most of the weight sits. The straps can also be adjusted around and over the head, so there’s enough flexibility to get a good fit if you’re sitting upright.
What we don’t love
![Controller unit and Shark Cyroglow LED face mask on a wooden countertop.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8af02e21e0dc0ec958594695fc96250256fb97c5/546_0_2100_1680/master/2100.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
Sadly, the main gripe I have with the Shark CryoGlow is one of its key selling points. Although I enjoy the calming effect of the undereye coolers, I found the weight of the mask made them dig into the delicate skin in that area. Whether I used the clip-on adjusters or not, I couldn’t bear lying down in the mask, as it was too heavy. The cooling pad positioning also meant the undereyes didn’t get any LED treatment.
Another frustration was that the cooling pads have fans that create a constant whirring sound, which is noisy and distracting during treatment. The coolers can be deactivated by turning the dial on the controller, but reactivating them is just as easy. I’ve accidentally knocked the dial countless times, causing the cooling fans to roar into action. Even when switched off immediately, they take a minute or so to quieten down again.
![Closeup of the controller unit of the Shark CryoGlow LED face mask.](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/8504f291d428e3404e39543e52f72573d7486dbd/648_0_1680_1680/master/1680.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
That’s a shame, since the controller is generally well designed; the scroll wheel and buttons make it easy to browse the settings, and the clip is helpful, if a little insecure. If Shark could change the cooling controls to a button, that would improve the design.
While the CryoGlow’s Better Ageing mode is great for early signs of ageing, it doesn’t have the most deeply penetrating wavelength – deep near-infrared – for more powerful anti-ageing. Deep near-infrared is becoming more common among new releases, although they tend to cost more. However, the Silk’n LED face mask Pro I tested has deep near-infrared and costs just £265 at full price. Of course, the LED industry is growing at a rate of knots, so it’s hard for Shark to keep up with all the latest features, but I’m surprised that its newest release, the Shark CryoGlow Plus, hasn’t added this (although battery life and LED coverage have improved).
Warranty and repairs
The device is guaranteed for two years if you register your device online within 28 days. This covers the cost of a repair or replacement mask if you have any problems during that time. Shark also offers troubleshooting advice online, or you can contact its customer service helpline (0800 862 0453).
Coincidentally, I tested this repairs service earlier this year when my sister bought a faulty CryoGlow mask at Christmas. After complaining, she had a new mask sent to her within a week (albeit in a different colour due to stock levels).
Should I buy the Shark CryoGlow LED mask?
If you want an effective LED mask that can treat multiple skin concerns at once, without adding extra light settings that aren’t as well-researched, then yes. And if puffy undereyes are a concern, you’ll be able to treat those as well.
The mask has given me good results, with daily breakouts minimised and unavoidable hormonal breakouts lasting less time than before. I found that the red light settings helped maintain a more even skin tone and a brighter complexion overall. And, notwithstanding its weight, its plastic build feels much sturdier than many silicone options.
I hate that the cooling patches cover the undereye, though. If you want an LED mask you can lie down in like a lizard in the sun, this weighty mask isn’t for you. Equally, if loud whirring noises in your ears are likely to annoy you, I’d steer clear. You’d be better off investing in a soft silicone mask such as the CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy mask – my new favourite overall. It may cost more, but it’s lighter, more comfortable and has more penetrating deep near-infrared light.
For more, read the best LED face masks that are worth the hype and our CurrentBody Multi Light Therapy LED mask review
Sarah Matthews is a consumer journalist who specialises in health and beauty reviews. In her four years of product testing, she’s worked her way through countless hair styling tools, hair removal, light therapy and skincare innovations. She’s seen beauty trends come and go, and can sniff out a fad from a gamechanger (that doesn’t mean she’s disciplined enough to always follow her own advice, though)
summary: The Shark CryoGlow LED face mask is a mid-priced skincare device featuring 160 LEDs across three wavelengths and unique electric undereye cooling pads. After extensive testing over two years and 100 treatments, the reviewer found it effective for reducing breakouts and calming inflammation, but noted drawbacks such as its heavy weight, noisy cooling fans, and lack of deep near-infrared wavelengths. Ultimately, while it is a sturdy and multi-functional option, the weight and cooling pad placement make it unsuitable for users who want to lie down during treatments.
key_points: The mask retails for £299.99 and features three preset LED modes (Better Ageing, Blemish Repair, and Skin Sustain) alongside adjustable electric undereye cooling.
Testing showed that the Blemish Repair mode effectively minimized breakouts and helped them heal faster.
Weighing 537g, the device is heavy and its cooling pads dig into delicate undereye skin while blocking LED treatment in that area.
The cooling fans create a constant whirring noise, and using the cooling feature significantly drains the battery life from 17 treatments down to seven.
The mask lacks the deeply penetrating near-infrared wavelengths found in some competing models.

title: Samsung Plans Major Free Feature Upgrade For Millions Of Galaxy Phones
author: Janhoi McGregor
content:
After originally launching with the Galaxy Z Fold 8 series on July 22nd alongside a host of new camera and AI agent skills, One UI 9 looks close to being released to millions of Galaxy phones, tablets and watches.
Samsung update tracker Tarun Vats spotted new One UI 9 beta builds for five different device families this week, including the Galaxy S26, Galaxy S25, Galaxy S24, Galaxy S25 FE and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic, all of which received new test builds within hours of each other.
The latest S26 build (ZZHC) suggests Samsung is preparing a sixth beta. The S25 build is the one most Galaxy owners have been waiting for. A new ZZHC build appearing on Samsung’s servers this week suggests the company is running final checks before opening the public program.
The S24 and S25 FE builds confirm both devices are progressing toward their own public beta programs.
The One UI 9 Timeline For Flagship Galaxy Phones
The Galaxy S26 series is the closest to a stable release. Beta 6 appears to be the next step after the fifth beta dropped last week, which was originally delayed.
The Galaxy S25 series public beta looks genuinely imminent. The internal build cleared Google Play Protect certification last week, and the new ZZHC build this week suggests Samsung is running final checks.
Once a build reaches this stage, it may be days rather than weeks before the public program opens. Galaxy S25, S25+ and S25 Ultra owners should check the Samsung Members app regularly for a beta invitation.
The Galaxy S24 series and Galaxy S25 FE are slightly behind but progressing. Both have new builds in testing, with public betas expected to follow the S25 program.
Samsung’s One UI 9.5 Is Already Being Planned
While One UI 9.0 is still rolling out, Samsung is already working on the next release. A leak spotted by tipster Fahad Ali Javed, via SamMobile ,reveals that One UI 9.5 is being developed with a "My Custom Widget" feature that allows users to pull data from Samsung apps like Calendar and Messages into a personalised widget with a modular layout. It’s likely based on Android 17's own Create Your Own Widget tool.
One UI 9 will ship with minimal design changes, but One UI 9.5 looks set to bring the major visual overhaul when it lands on the Galaxy S27 next year.
What You Get In Samsung’s One UI 9 Update
The headline new features are Now Nudge, which proactively suggests the next logical action based on what you’re doing, like opening your calendar when you’re texting about a plan. There’s also My FanCam, which lets you film a wide crowd shot and then go back to spotlight a specific person in the Gallery app.
Photo Assist now accepts voice instructions rather than typed requests. AI Privacy Alerts flag apps that are over-accessing location data or running background permissions they shouldn't need, and a new AI Assistant Activity log shows exactly which apps your AI has accessed and when.
Horizontal Lock, one of the Galaxy S26's camera highlights, is also coming to the S25 series via One UI 9 according to internal builds spotted by SammyFans.
The Quick Panel has been redesigned with more customisation options. There's also an improved Bixby that can answer questions about the device and complete tasks like turning on a mobile hotspot when asked in natural language.
It's hard to know which devices get which features, as some will be reserved for current flagships to differentiate between newer and older devices.
Samsung’s own teaser for the Galaxy S26 FE suggests MyFanCam and Horizontal Lock are coming to that device, which suggests Samsung isn’t reserving those features exclusively for the S26 flagship line. This is likely good news for S25 and S24 owners waiting on the same update.
Which Samsung Phones Get Gemini Intelligence Via One UI 9?
Not every phone getting One UI 9 will get all of it. The Galaxy S26 FE launching on August 27th could become the first Galaxy device to ship with One UI 9 but without Gemini Intelligence. This is Google's new agentic AI toolkit that completes actions on your behalf with minimal input. Google's official requirements list 12GB of RAM as the minimum, and the S26 FE is expected to launch with 8GB.
Samsung and Google have both declined to confirm where exactly the Gemini Intelligence cutoff falls. The S26 FE’s launch next week will answer that question for millions of Galaxy owners wondering whether their device will get Samsung and Google’s most important AI feature in One UI 9.
summary: Samsung is preparing to release the One UI 9 public beta for multiple Galaxy device families, including the S26, S25, S24, S25 FE, and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic. The upcoming update brings new features such as proactive AI suggestions, voice-controlled Photo Assist, privacy alerts, and a redesigned Quick Panel. Additionally, Samsung is already developing One UI 9.5, which is expected to feature a major visual overhaul and custom widget tools.
key_points: New One UI 9 test builds have been spotted for the Galaxy S26, S25, S24, S25 FE, and Galaxy Watch 8 Classic.
One UI 9 features include Now Nudge AI suggestions, voice instructions for Photo Assist, AI Privacy Alerts, and an improved Bixby.
Samsung is already working on One UI 9.5, which is slated to introduce a major visual overhaul and a 'My Custom Widget' feature.
The Galaxy S26 FE may launch with One UI 9 but could lack Gemini Intelligence due to an 8GB RAM limitation.

title: 7 developers that will save the video games industry - Reader’s Feature
author: GameCentral
content:
![Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 screenshot of main characters](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_308351949-063b.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&w=646) 
With big publishers currently doing their best to destroy the games industry, a reader lists seven smaller developers who are helping to make things better.
I won’t go over them all again, but there’s no denying that the video game industry is facing plenty of problems right now. Thankfully, though, there are still plenty of reasons to be excited about the future.
Developers like Nintendo and FromSoftware will continue doing what they do best and even the likes of Capcom are enjoying something of a renaissance, reviving some of its most beloved franchises alongside experimenting with new IPs like the entertaining Pragmata.
Looking beyond these big name studios, however, there are countless talented developers quietly doing their thing and delivering some truly fantastic games. From ambitious indies to smaller studios punching well above their weight, there’s plenty to be excited about. So, here are just a few of the developers giving us reason to feel optimistic.
11 bit studios
Expert, exclusive gaming analysis
A Polish developer founded in 2010, 11 bit studios first came to prominence with the release of This War Of Mine in 2014, a game that showed the darker side of war that video games usually avoid and often forced players into making difficult decisions that went beyond the standard good vs. evil. Their next two games, both in the Frostpunk series, expanded these ideas to a larger scale and mixed city building with survival elements as the player attempted to keep the population alive in a world decimated by climate change.
Hot on the heels of this came The Alters, arguably their most ambitious project, that found a space miner trapped on an alien planet and having to do anything they could to survive. Having also helped publish some other small budget titles, including the very good Death Howl, it appears they’ll be returning to the world of Frostpunk for their next game and it’ll be interesting to see how they develop the series.
AdHoc Studios
Founded by former Telltale Games staff, following the company’s bankruptcy in 2018, AdHoc Studios is an American video game developer that produced one of the best games of last year in Dispatch. Using what they learned from their years of working on narrative-focused adventures, they took the animation, script, and voice-acting to a whole new level and set a standard for the genre that will be hard to follow.
Having announced a partnership with Critical Role Productions they are now working on a game set in the fantasy world of Exandria, and one would imagine it’ll hit the same high standards as their last game.
Daniel Mullins Games
Daniel Mullins started his career by taking part in game jams – events where participants have to create a video game from scratch in a given period of time – before releasing his first commercial project Pony Island in 2016. Each of his subsequent games (The Hex and Inscryption) retained the same meta narrative and fourth wall breaking dimensions whilst experimenting with different genres, making for some of the most unique games of the last decade. With Pony Island 2 on the horizon, it seems Daniel Mullins isn’t out of ideas just yet.
Hazelight Studios
A Swedish developer founded in 2014, Hazelight Studios have found their own little niche with co-operative multiplayer games that generously only require one player to own the game. Starting with A Way Out, it was really It Takes Two and then Split Fiction that put them on the map with the inventive asynchronous powers given to each player keeping things fresh for the games run time.
The success of Split Fiction in particular has secured their future and they’ve announced that they’re now working on a new game.
Larian Studios
An independent studio from Belgium, Larian Studios is best known for creating role-playing games, since they were founded back in 1996. Having released numerous relatively well received titles in the Divinity series, it was Divinity: Original Sin and Divinity: Original Sin 2 that really saw Larian hone their craft before the incredible Baldur’s Gate 3 took the genre to a whole new level in terms of storytelling and player freedom.
Having decided against creating any DLC for Baldur’s Gate 3, or a fourth title in the series, Larian have announced that they will be returning to the Divinity series and if it lives up to their last few titles it’ll be something very special indeed.
Sandfall Interactive
A French video game development company founded in 2020 by former Ubisoft employees that had become disillusioned with working for a big studio, the heads of Sandfall Interactive immediately began working on a role-playing game that ‘they themselves would like to play.’
The result was, of course, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, a game with an immersive story, original combat system and incredible music that exceeded all expectations and swept up pretty much every video game award going last year. No announcement has been made as to what their next game will be, but rumours suggest it could be set in the same painted world as Clair Obscur and that is a world rife with possibilities.
Supergiant Games
An independent developer based in San Francisco, Supergiant games cut their teeth with the well-received Bastion and Transistor before truly announcing themselves with Hades, arguably the best rougelike game ever made. Four years later they followed that up with Hades 2 that whilst following a very similar template refined the formula to make for another excellent title. They haven’t currently announced what their next game will be, but whether it’s Hades 3 or something new, I’ll be there on launch day.
There are plenty of other developers I could have mentioned here, so let me know which studios you think are worth a mention.
