All Rights Reserved (Picture: Fabio Lovino)](https://metro.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/SEI_309021192-0ff4.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=493px%2C396px%2C1621px%2C913px&resize=646%2C363)
- Holly Willoughby just wants to see 'normal fannies' in porn
- ‘The sickest film ever made’ gets rare UK release
- PlayStation fans prepare for PS5 boycott – here's when to switch off
By reader drlowdon
The reader’s features do not necessarily represent the views of GameCentral or Metro.
You can submit your own 500 to 600-word reader feature at any time, which if used will be published in the next appropriate weekend slot.
Just contact us at gamecentral@metro.co.uk or use our Submit Stuff page and you won’t need to send an email.
summary: While major publishers face criticism, various smaller and independent video game developers are delivering exceptional titles and driving the industry forward. A reader feature highlights seven such studios—including 11 bit studios, AdHoc Studios, Daniel Mullins Games, Hazelight Studios, Larian Studios, Sandfall Interactive, and Supergiant Games—that continue to inspire optimism through innovative and ambitious projects. These developers have gained acclaim for pushing narrative boundaries, inventing unique co-operative mechanics, and creating award-winning role-playing and rogue-like games.
key_points: 11 bit studios is recognized for thought-provoking games like This War Of Mine, the Frostpunk series, and The Alters.
AdHoc Studios, founded by former Telltale Games staff, set a high standard for narrative-focused adventures with Dispatch.
Hazelight Studios carved out a niche in co-op multiplayer with titles like It Takes Two and Split Fiction that only require one copy to play.
Larian Studios achieved widespread acclaim and elevated the RPG genre with Divinity: Original Sin and Baldur’s Gate 3.
Sandfall Interactive and Supergiant Games have delivered major hits, with Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 and the Hades series respectively.

title: How Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro Launch Date Crushes The Competition
author: Ewan Spence
content:
Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro family on Wednesday, Sept. 9. Give or take a few days, this is the predictable launch window of every new iPhone. It’s also a date that allows Apple to be aggressive; the competition knows the date, knows what’s coming down the line, and is forced to avoid it as best they can. Apple’s preferred iPhone launch date is one of the most aggressive moves that the Cupertino business makes each year.
The iPhone 18 Pro And The Mid-Range Squeeze At IFA Berlin
Apple’s early-September iPhone 18 Pro launch systematically deprives IFA Berlin exhibitors of media oxygen, while mid-range Android devices face severe component margin pressure.
This year, IFA Berlin takes place from Sept. 4 to Sept. 8. Since 2005, it has taken place annually and is seen by many smartphone manufacturers as an opportunity to launch new hardware, akin to an “end-of-year Mobile World Congress.” While IFA is not exclusively for smartphones, it has seen key launch events in recent years, such as last year’s Galaxy S25 FE.
It’s not the best venue for launching premium handsets, even with the world’s press in attendance. The portfolio of new launches benefits mid-range handsets more than the flagships. That may offer IFA a slight advantage this year as Apple moves the vanilla iPhone 18 to spring 2027, putting similar pressure on MWC. Yet mid-range handsets are under the most financial pressure due to rising prices and lower stock levels of memory and storage across the production chain, making them a bet with far less return now that Apple has moved into the premium space.
The iPhone 18 Pro Has The Last-Mover Advantage Over Premium Android Phones
Samsung and Google are forced to compress their hardware release cycles to avoid direct marketing collisions with Apple’s dominant fourth-quarter iPhone timetable.
Apple has effectively secured a last-mover advantage in the premium space. Samsung has repeatedly delayed the launch of the Galaxy Z Foldable range to give it as much time as possible to become established before the iPhone arrives. Google has a similar choice to make on the Pixel, with just two weeks between the reviews of the Pixel 11 Pro arriving and the reveal of the iPhone 18 Pro to the world’s press; a moment that will hand Apple all the digital headlines and column inches it can handle.
Whether competing smartphones choose to avoid the iPhone and move further away from the commercially rich fourth quarter, or launch closer to and accept any momentum is going to be squashed once Apple’s smartphone neuters their efforts, the true winner is Apple. The iPhone 18 Pro can clear the bases when it launches, allowing incoming CEO John Ternus to start out with a continuity product which will dominate retail shelves.
iPhone 18 Pro Carrier Subsidies And Retail Dominance
North American carrier upgrade cycles align directly with Apple's September retail calendar, starving competing Android flagships of carrier marketing support.
Apple’s release of the iPhone, particularly in North America, sweeps away the competition on so many levels. It smothers other launch events and PR activities as it launches its own phone. With notable traffic boosts over the Android competition guaranteeing more digital inches and headlines, the associated media coverage drowns out alternatives.
With so many consumers locked into 12- or 24-month smartphone contracts that end just as the next iPhone hits retail shelves, carriers’ PR campaigns around the iPhone help bring customers back for another contract.
The Fixed iPhone 18 Pro Calendar Is An Unmatched Moat
Apple is locked into an early September release date for many reasons. Even knowing that, the competition has not found a simple way to match the elephant in the room. Apple will quite happily take advantage of this fixed launch date and the pressure it can apply to the wider smartphone ecosystem. The launch date of the iPhone 18 Pro remains a red-letter day for the industry.
summary: Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro family around Wednesday, September 9, utilizing a predictable early-September window that aggressively dominates the smartphone market. This fixed launch date deprives events like IFA Berlin of media attention, forces Android competitors like Samsung and Google to alter their release cycles, and aligns with North American carrier upgrade schedules. Consequently, Apple secures a major last-mover advantage and retail dominance that effectively sidelines competing flagships and mid-range devices.
key_points: Apple is expected to launch the iPhone 18 Pro family on or around September 9, leveraging a predictable early-September release window.
The timing systematically deprives IFA Berlin exhibitors of media oxygen and pressures mid-range Android devices.
Competitors like Samsung and Google must compress their hardware release cycles to avoid direct marketing collisions with Apple.
North American carrier upgrade cycles align with the September release, starving competing Android flagships of carrier marketing support.

title: Kazunori Yamauchi Says Tire Physics Remain One of Gran Turismo’s Biggest Challenges
author: Jordan Greer
content:
![](https://www.gtplanet.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/porsche-gt7-oldvictory-800x450.webp)
British motoring magazine evo has published a wide-ranging interview with Gran Turismo creator Kazunori Yamauchi, covering everything from the challenges of tire physics to Polyphony Digital’s relationship with Sony.
It was conducted at the FAT Ice Race in Zell am See, Austria, earlier this year, where Yamauchi joined Polestar as the company continued its promotional tie-in between the Polestar 5 and Gran Turismo 7.
Much of the ground covered will be familiar to GTPlanet readers, but there are a few comments worth digging into, including an interesting one about the pressure Yamauchi used to face from Sony.
Sony Pushback Has Eased
![](https://www.gtplanet.net/wp-content/uploads/2010/06/gran-turismo-5-e3-2010-screenshots-3.jpeg)
When asked whether he has ever been told by his bosses at Sony to cut corners or that his team is taking too long to produce new games, Yamauchi gave an answer that will raise eyebrows among anyone who followed the series through the late 2000s: “Up to about Gran Turismo 5, yes. Nowadays, not so much.”
Of course, Gran Turismo 5 had one of the most protracted and publicly scrutinized development cycles in the series’ history with two significant announced delays, so it’s interesting to hear Yamauchi acknowledge that corporate patience was being tested during that era.
Yamauchi also repeated the now-familiar figure that a single car takes roughly eight months to complete. That covers both the graphics model and the physics work required to make it behave like the real thing, compared to roughly two hours per car back in the original Gran Turismo days. Recreating the Nürburgring Nordschleife, he said, took four years.
Tires Remain the Hardest Problem
![](https://www.gtplanet.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/caterham-dunlop-gt7-800x450.webp)
On the simulation side, Yamauchi was frank about where the biggest challenge lies: tires.
Components like suspension and drivetrains can be modeled with little gap between simulation and reality, but tires are a different story, with some of the finer details difficult to pin down even when working with tire manufacturers. The specific difficulty is the contact patch, and how its behavior shifts with heat, wear, and surface conditions.
“The level of grain that happens when you have certain conditions on the track, it’s something that we just don’t have yet,” Yamauchi admitted.
This challenge has been going on for a while. Yamauchi described tire modeling as Gran Turismo’s most difficult simulation challenge as far back as 2017 when he accepted his honorary doctorate degree in Modena, Italy.
![](https://www.gtplanet.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/gt7-gameupdate-171-caterham-002-20260820-800x450.jpg)
Although Yamauchi made these comments to evo earlier this year, this week’s Update 1.71 brought yet another revision to the tire physics algorithm, including changes to slip behavior, rolling resistance, heating, wear, and grip loss. Neither update’s notes mention the contact-patch behavior or graining, suggesting those remain areas of development.
Modern cars aren’t making the job any easier. Electronic management systems for drivetrains and differentials vary substantially from car to car and manufacturer to manufacturer, and EVs push the required level of detail higher still.
Yamauchi cited the Polestar 5’s behavior on ice as markedly different from a Porsche Taycan. He also said he personally test drives the cars at the end of the development process as a final check before they are added to Gran Turismo 7.
How Cars Make the Cut
![](https://www.gtplanet.net/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/twingos-gt7-800x450.jpg)
Yamauchi reiterated that Gran Turismo’s car list isn’t planned through any single process.
Some cars come about when manufacturers approach Polyphony with new models, while others are models Yamauchi himself simply wants to include, and player requests can tip the balance too. He says community feedback has drawn his attention to cars he might otherwise have overlooked, including the continuing appetite for ’90s Japanese machinery and more utilitarian vehicles.
As for which manufacturers he has turned down? “I cannot answer,” was the reply, delivered with what evo describes as a wry smile.
The interview also touches on the audience playing Gran Turismo today, which Yamauchi says spans teenagers to players over 60, and the pattern of early Gran Turismo players growing up to hold senior positions within car manufacturers themselves (something he has spoken about before).
Polestar’s head of brand, Michael Manske, added a notable figure of his own, telling evo that 160,000 players signed up to drive the Polestar 5 during its GT7 time-trial campaign. That kind of exposure is exactly why Polestar leaned so heavily on Gran Turismo for the 5’s launch.
The full interview first appeared in evo issue 348. It’s now available on the magazine’s website and is well worth reading in full.
See more articles on Kazunori Yamauchi.
summary: In an interview with motoring magazine evo, Gran Turismo creator Kazunori Yamauchi discussed development challenges, noting that pressure and pushback from Sony have eased significantly since the era of Gran Turismo 5. He highlighted tire physics as the game's most difficult simulation challenge, particularly due to the complexities of modeling the contact patch under various conditions. Yamauchi also shared details on how cars are selected for the game, combining manufacturer input, personal preference, and community feedback.
key_points: Kazunori Yamauchi stated that corporate pressure and pushback from Sony were significant up to Gran Turismo 5, but have since eased.
Tire physics and modeling the contact patch behavior remain Gran Turismo's biggest simulation challenges.
Developing a single car takes roughly eight months, while recreating the Nürburgring Nordschleife took four years.
Car selection for the game is driven by manufacturer requests, Yamauchi's personal choices, and community feedback.

title: Gorgeous and hazy pixel art horror farming sim Neverway has been pushed to 2027, but you can at least have a gander at some of the NPCs you can smooch
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Sorry folks, some bad news: Neverway, the horror life sim and RPG combo from one of the artists behind Celeste and the composer of Fez, has been delayed into 2027. While it never had an exact release date anyway, developer Coldblood Inc. shared word of the delay in a Steam blog post earlier this week.
"Our process has always been about understanding what you, as a player, are feeling when you play the game and making sure that aligns with the story. Seeing how the prologue resonated with so many of you, along with internal playtests, inspired us on how the later parts of Neverway could take shape," explains the blog post. "This means some of the original chapters and areas grew in a way we hope will meet your expectations. We believe in this game's potential, which is why we decided to take this extra time to make it the very best version it can be. And don’t worry, we don’t plan on growing it any more than that. As much as we love working on Neverway, we know you’re excited to play it too and don’t want to delay it again."
While I'm sure it'll be a disappointment to some, the devs (of which there are only three, "plus a few collaborators," so make sure you cut them some slack) offered a bit of a peek behind the curtain to tide us all over. For one, across the game's 20 characters there's more than 250 routines that they follow, so good luck to the wiki contributors on that front. Speaking of those characters, you can romance 12 of them! Not at once, I think, no mention of that, but at the very least separately. Some wonderful portraits can be seen over on the aforementioned blog post, so do give 'em a look.
Developing relationships with those characters does still sound important however, as it's also been revealed that Neverway will have multiple endings, and your bonds "may be directly tied to the ending of the game…" Coldblood further explain that "Some are good. Or maybe evil. Depends on your point of view. We are trying to avoid “bad endings” and just making them interesting in different ways!"
It all sounds like it's coming together quite nicely, just needs a tad more time! And while you wait, you can wishlist it on Steam, where there's also a demo for you to try out if you fancy.
summary: The pixel art horror farming sim and RPG Neverway, developed by Coldblood Inc., has been delayed to 2027 so the team can expand certain chapters and areas. Despite the delay, the developers shared new details about the game's features, including its 20 characters, 12 romanceable NPCs, and multiple endings tied to player bonds. A demo is currently available on Steam for players to try while they wait.
key_points: Neverway has been delayed into 2027 to allow the developers time to expand original chapters and areas.
The game features 20 characters who follow over 250 routines and includes 12 romanceable NPCs.
Player relationships with characters are directly tied to the game's multiple endings.
A demo for Neverway is currently available on Steam for players to try.

title: "We're in danger of making this a regular thing" - What have you been playing this week?
author: Robert Purchese
content:
22nd August
Hello and welcome back to our regular feature where we write a little about the games we've been playing. This week, Mat J gets philosophical on us; Connor plays Minesweeper for some reason; and Bertie rallies the wonderful Eurogamer readers for a second week of Big Walk wholesome hilarity.
What have you been playing this week?
Here's another question: do you remember what you were playing last week? You don't have to! The What We've Been Playing archive has you covered.
Sobosuba, PC
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/i_1MX82FkmQ/hqdefault.jpg) sobosuba - Official trailer
If you don't spend a lot of time on Bluesky, a conversation about games that play themselves might have slipped the corners of your vision. If you'd like to read the inciting observation then head over to Jank. The argument's compelling enough: how much are we actually playing a video game that largely plays itself? What are we getting out of the experience if we don't really need to be that involved?
Critic Chris Franklin would point out this is a type of deconstruction which only really used to be levied at narrative games, that the absence of meaningful player interaction was in knowing the experience could only end along a predetermined path. It's new to extend that line of thinking to something like Vampire Survivors, where the goal is to reposition yourself for 30 minutes and essentially just select items you think will allow that to continue.
If you want to, you can probably apply this to any game. For instance: you just stack blocks on top of each other and make lines of them that disappear so you can keep doing it? Or: you chuck orbs at the other orbs at the top of the screen and if they're the right colour they fall down? You could probably do this for being alive if you really wanted - it's all just breathing in and out, is it?
Anyway! In sobosuba you merge little blobs together. It's like that game where you merge types of fruit together. The blobs get bigger the more matches you make, and they've got soft-body physics so they'll all wobble about. I hate it; I've been playing it all week.
-Mat J
Minesweeper, mobile
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/aKML1EbVCvY/hqdefault.jpg) Minesweeper Expert World Record in 28.84 by Ze-En Ju (JZE)
I was out of data for like two whole days this week! What a nightmare. It forced me back to the old faithful, the tried-and-true: Minesweeper. The gaming equivalent of playing with rocks you find on the ground during a power cut.
It really is a brilliant little game. A puzzle where you try to find mines hidden in a big grid using numbers to work out how likely nearby they are. Trying to speak about minesweeper in 2026 is hilarious because it's a known quantity: everyone knows the deal.
Nonetheless, there's this brilliant moment in Minesweeper where the numbers just make sense, and you can pick out safe spaces with just a quick glance. I love seeing a big red three next to three clickable spots. I love it when you click a safe spot and a massive patch gets unlocked.
-Connor
Big Walk, PC
We managed a week-two! The Eurogamer readers - you Eurogamer readers - and I took to Big Walk for a second week of extraordinary adventures. I wrote about our previous Big Walk adventures for Optimism Week, in case you're curious. With a third adventure planned Tuesday 25th evening (you are more than welcome to join, just pop into the Eurogamer Discord) we're in danger of making this a regular thing.
This week, with a bit more experience, we broke into two teams of four-ish people ostensibly to cover more ground and solve more puzzles. We sort of did that. We found a megaphone, which was a mistake; we hacked our way up a rocky cliff by alternately picking each other up and throwing people, and then got lost; and we made a tower of people sitting on fold-out chairs, for no apparent reason other than a nice screenshot. But we actually Achieve with a capital A, and do some stuff, like turn the chair lift on and the train, choo choo. Bleeuaah bleeauaah? It makes a hilariously horrid noise.
There are too many micro-stories and moments to share - Big Walk is a game of such things, of being beside people, of noticing together - but I continue to be impressed by how generous a package it is. There is a whole world here, an island playground, and it's just dense enough to provide things to do without giving you so much to do that you fill your time doing rather than being. Big Walk is about being around people and enjoying that.
Can I also just quickly praise the puzzles? My partner - who was in the other group - told me about a puzzle that involved just, well, sitting together - I don't want to say too much! Without anything to actually do, people simply talked, she said, talking about their lives and themselves. I find that remarkable - subtly, quietly, unremarkably remarkable. Which other game encourages that?
Around that, I've dabbled in The Lord of the Rings: The War in the North - surprisingly enjoyable - and had some decent runs in Hades 2.
-Bertie
summary: Eurogamer staff share the various video games they have been playing recently, ranging from philosophical discussions about games that play themselves to classic puzzles and multiplayer adventures. Mat J explores soft-body physics in the blob-merging game sobosuba, while Connor turns to mobile Minesweeper after running out of data. Meanwhile, Bertie recounts a second week of community adventures in Big Walk alongside dabbling in other titles like Hades 2.
key_points: Mat J discusses the philosophical debate around games that largely play themselves while reviewing the blob-merging game sobosuba.
Connor plays mobile Minesweeper after running out of data for two days, praising its classic puzzle mechanics.
Bertie organizes a second week of multiplayer sessions in Big Walk with Eurogamer readers on Discord.
Bertie also briefly mentions dabbling in The Lord of the Rings: The War in the North and Hades 2.

title: Pixel 11 Pro XL review: Snappier cameras can't hide an iterative upgrade | TechCrunch
author: Ivan Mehta
content:
If you buy the new Pixel 11 Pro, you might have to proactively tell people that you bought the latest phone, unless they are following each and every launch. The main reason is that the Pixel 11 doesn’t look that different from prior models. The main updates to its aesthetics are its new colors, which are admittedly gorgeous, and the addition of a small glowing light on the back of the phone, which has limited use.
The phone arrives with some new Gemini features, but I’m not sure if AI chops are attracting customers to buy new phones these days. In daily use, what you may notice is that the Pixel 11 Pro’s cameras are snappier, and there are more options for you to customize the way your photos look. Otherwise, the Pixel 11 Pro XL feels like the previous-gen phone had a big Pixel Drop update.
I have used the Obsidian Pixel 11 Pro XL for nearly a week, and so far, I can say that despite the relatively iterative updates, the phone is still solid and feels good to use.
Rambler
Rambler is one of my favorite new features on the Pixel 11 Pro XL. This new, AI-powered dictation tool takes out filler words like “um” and “ah” and formats your speech. The feature directly takes on other dictation apps like Wispr and Willow.
![A photo of Google's dictation tool called Rambler](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/1787295676463.jpg?w=680)
The dictation tool also handles switching between languages and noisy environments well.
Though it might make its way to some other devices, if you have a Pixel, this is a very cool and useful feature that you could end up using daily, compared with some of the other AI features.
For the last year, I have used dictation tools frequently to take quick notes, reply to emails, and messages on devices that I use. Google’s tool is on par with a few of the top tools in the industry, I found. (The tool is so good that I have pretty much rambled my way into writing this section without needing any edits!)
Gemini updates
I’ve just had the phone for five days, so the Proactive Suggestions feature, designed to surface context-aware suggestions from apps, didn’t yet show up everywhere. I did see it when I conversed with friends over text messages, when they were asking me about my schedule. My only gripe is that I’d want Gemini to know about all my calendars, not just Google’s, and suggest my availability based on that.
Suggestions also don’t always show up. For instance, when someone asked for my address, Gemini should have picked that up from my emails, but it didn’t.
In addition, Gemini offers agentic capabilities that can help you with completing some tasks, such as placing a food order for you. But this feature is available in the U.S., and as I am based in India, I couldn’t test it.
The new Live Translate feature is useful for when you are watching a live stream or a video without translated captions. However, you will need to download specific languages.
HiLight is not really a highlight
One of Google’s marketing messages this year was about how it designed Pixel to make you look at your screen less.
The company has only one feature to show for it called HiLight, an LED notification light on the back of the phone that replaced last year’s temperature sensor. The feature allows you to keep your phone face down, while delivering subtle alerts by way of the light.
The light itself looks cool when active as it lights up in green, yellow, pink, purple, or white. But a big limitation is that it only works when you activate Gemini or get phone calls from your favorite contacts, not texts.
The light can also indicate that Gemini is listening or thinking. This may be useful to know that Gemini is processing information after you have asked it to execute a complex task. But besides that, I can only think of a few scenarios when my phone is face down, and I’m not wearing any earbuds to listen for the activation sound, but still need to know if Gemini is active.
![](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Pixel-HiLight.jpg?w=680)
Besides, for favorite callers, you can always set a special ringtone. There may be only a few occasions when your phone is on silent, and if you haven’t set up calls from close people to get through, and you are paying attention to a light on the back of the phone.
This feature is ripe for future customization, however, so hopefully it continues to be developed. I would like to one day choose a color for when I get a text or WhatsApp message from my contacts. Plus, if I can assign different colors for different apps, I would know if I need to pick up my phone or if I can tackle that task later.
Pixel’s cameras are snappy
Google decided to opt for a larger sensor for both the main and the telephoto sensors compared with the Pixel 10 Pro XL. On paper, this change means cameras can let in more light and, in turn, capture more details. (I didn’t pixel-peep to confirm this). However, thanks to the new processor and software updates, the camera app and capture feel snappy, and you can take photos faster.
Google also made Night Sight, its low-light photography mode, faster, which means you don’t have to hold the phone with the subject in focus for as long and can more easily avoid blurry photos.

Google’s Pro Res Zoom feature, which uses AI to upscale some parts of the photo when you go above 30x digital zoom on Pro XL, has been improved. The maximum zoom level was 100x last year, and now it is 120x. It is tough to keep your hand steady and take a legible photo, even after all the AI magic, if the subject is across the street. But for a lower zoom range, you get a usable photo.
One of the marquee features of this year’s camera release is called Looks, which acts like filters, but Google claims that it’s changing the way the computational photography pipeline works on the phone.
There are four core default looks called original, natural, shadows, and vanilla that you can select from the settings menu. You can also switch between other Looks called editorial, classic (with more grain), digi (reminds you of old digital cameras), black tie, and minimal.

![](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260820_102210029_digi.jpg?w=511)
![](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260820_102133856_natural.jpg?w=511)
On the Pixel 11, one-touch quick access controls are customizable, so I could swap out white balance for ISO to appear directly. I could also quickly access Looks through this section and take photos in different styles.
Another new addition to the feature set is Magic Capture, which lets you initiate a video clip and use AI to pull out top moments from the clip that could be saved as photos. This is great for capturing wiggly things like babies or pets, or action shots, as in sports. There are a few limitations, though — the mode doesn’t do well with moving subjects and saves photos only in 12-megapixel resolution.
I have two cats and a dog, so I am going to use this feature frequently! I’ll leave you with a picture of my cat trying to catch a feather, saved by Magic Capture.
![](https://techcrunch.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/PXL_20260821_082453267.MC_-rotated.jpg?w=511)
Price
Unfortunately, the component crunch has forced hardware companies to raise device prices. Google scrapped the 128GB base model, and while it priced the 256GB model the same as last year’s version for the Pixel 11 and the Pixel 11 Pro, it reduced the RAM size from 16GB to 12GB for both.
The Pixel 11 Pro XL also got a $100 bump from last year’s price.
Because of this, the new Pixels don’t incentivize gadget enthusiasts to upgrade from last year’s phone, despite being solid devices. The camera improvements are notable, and Rambler is great, but some of this will likely trickle down to older Pixels in the future.
summary: The Pixel 11 Pro XL is largely an iterative upgrade that looks very similar to prior models, featuring mostly aesthetic updates and minor aesthetic tweaks. However, it introduces useful additions like the AI-powered Rambler dictation tool, snappier cameras with new computational photography styles called Looks, and faster Night Sight. Despite being a solid and reliable device, price increases, reduced RAM sizes, and limited functionality for features like the HiLight notification LED make it a tough sell for users upgrading from last year's model.
key_points: The Pixel 11 Pro XL features minimal design changes from prior models, offering mostly new colors and a limited back notification light called HiLight.
Rambler is a standout AI-powered dictation tool that effectively removes filler words and handles noisy environments well.
Camera improvements include snappier capture times, faster Night Sight, an increased digital zoom up to 120x, and a new 'Looks' feature for alternative photo styles.
Google increased the price of the Pixel 11 Pro XL by $100 and reduced the RAM size from 16GB to 12GB on lower configurations.

title: Raise up a mech pilot and make sure she doesn't get Evangelion-level depressed in the sci-fi visual novel Valkyrie Iteration: Mecha Pilot Raising Pocket Simulator
author: Oisin Kuhnke
content:
Raising sims aren't a genre I've partaken in, partially because so many of them are geared towards a sort of father, daughter vibe that doesn't quite fit me. Raising a mech pilot, however, seems like something a bit more my speed, so you won't be surprised to hear of my interest in Valkyrie Iteration: Mecha Pilot Raising Pocket Simulator, a visual novel with a name that seems to do what it says in the tin.
In Valkyrie Iteration (of course I'm not writing the title out in full every time), you are a technomaster, which in this case sounds like a handler from Armored Core over a sonically proficient beat producing aficionado. You have been put in charge of training Lana alongside her sentient mech, the titular Valkyrie. Except, ruh roh! "The Valkyrie’s power threatens to consume her very essence." Classic mech stuff, right there.
![Cover image for YouTube video](https://i.ytimg.com/vi/XI8S9TGBbAI/hqdefault.jpg) Demo is available // Valkyrie Iteration: Mecha Pilot Raising Pocket Simulator
There's a lot to balance in Valkyrie Iteration. For one, you have to plan Lana's daily schedule, like whether she's training, resting, or just having a chat, all of which helps to develop her skills, mental health, and bond with her mech. You also have to keep her synchronization and strength in check in case she gets too fatigued or flat out depressed in order to make sure she's ready to head out on missions.
The story sounds like your usual sci-fi, mecha affair. In a far flung future, some strange, law of nature defying, alternate dimension beings called Phantoms rock up and start attacking us humans. In turn, humans decided there was no other option to build mechs (right they are), which are the Valkyries, all of which come complete with their own soul. You can feel the Evangelion influence oozing here, a series that has its own history with raising sims.
It all looks quite neat, and there's a demo to have a go at too if you fancy, which you can check out on Steam (or just give it a wishlist if you're strapped for time).
summary: Valkyrie Iteration: Mecha Pilot Raising Pocket Simulator is a sci-fi visual novel where players act as technomasters training a mech pilot named Lana and her sentient mecha, the Valkyrie. Players must manage Lana's daily schedule, mental health, synchronization, and strength to prepare her for missions against alternate-dimension beings known as Phantoms. A playable demo of the game is currently available on Steam.
key_points: Players take on the role of a technomaster in charge of training a pilot named Lana.
The Valkyrie mech possesses its own soul, and its power threatens to consume Lana's essence.
Gameplay involves balancing Lana's schedule between training, resting, and chatting to manage her skills and mental health.
Humanity fights alternate-dimension beings called Phantoms using specialized mechs.
A game demo is available to play on Steam.

title: Furious PS5 Players Unplug Their Consoles in Protest as Blackout Gets Underway
author: Push Square; Sammy Barker
content:
![Furious PS5 Players Unplug Their Consoles in Protest Against Sony 1](https://images.pushsquare.com/69d52814c6f59/furious-ps5-players-unplug-their-consoles-in-protest-against-sony-1.900x.jpg)
Irate PS5 players have started unplugging their consoles all around the world, as a protest against Sony gets underway.
The blackout – technically scheduled to start at 7pm local time, but already being observed by many participants – is designed to reduce the Japanese giant’s active users, a key performance metric for the company.
Campaigners suggest participants should keep their consoles unplugged from today through 30th August as a minimum. That means no logins, no gaming, and certainly no spending through the PS Store.
While the protest is primarily aimed at Sony’s decision to cease manufacturing physical discs in January 2028, organisers also argue that the company has grown “further apart from its fan base”.
Earlier this week, a Push Square poll concluded 92% of enthusiasts believe PS Studios would benefit from new management, after stories emerged it was rebooting development on spin-off game Horizon Hunters Gathering.
As of its most recent financial report, Sony attracted around 125 million monthly active users, an increase year-over-year. I think this number would have to drop precipitously to have any kind of effect.
Speaking with investors about potential boycotts and PS Plus cancellations, Sony’s CFO Lin Tao said it’s not seeing any “impact on our business”.
This organised and widely publicised blackout campaign may be protesters’ best opportunity to get the company’s attention, then. Will you be taking part?
summary: PlayStation 5 players worldwide have begun unplugging their consoles in a protest against Sony that runs through at least August 30th. The blackout aims to reduce Sony's active user metrics to protest the company's decision to end physical disc manufacturing by January 2028 and its perceived disconnection from fans. Despite the campaign, Sony's CFO stated that the company is not currently seeing any business impact from boycotts or cancellations.
key_points: PS5 players are participating in a global console blackout protest running from today through August 30th.
The protest is primarily driven by Sony's plan to stop manufacturing physical discs in January 2028.
Organizers want participants to avoid logging in, gaming, and spending money on the PS Store to lower active user metrics.
Sony's CFO reported that the company has seen no business impact from potential boycotts and PS Plus cancellations.

Gather materials and build your ultimate territory, but be prepared to defend your home against relentless sieges. In this world, your enemies are your greatest asset."

- Comfy Corners: Unpack and Decorate (August 26): "Design the apartment of your dreams in a relaxing and meditative experience focused on creativity, comfort, and personal expression."
- Hidden Cats in Barcelona (August 26): "It’s time to have a snack at a local Churreria and take a long stroll through Park Güell, because the Hidden Cats have arrived in ever beautiful and sunny Cat-alonia!"

- NBA 2K27 Deluxe Edition (August 26): "The hustle doesn’t stop and the run never ends in NBA 2K27. Chase greatness around the clock in MyCAREER, MyTEAM, and MyNBA, and make your hoop dreams a reality."
- Aggelos 2 (August 27): "Aggelos 2 is an explosive action-platformer where lightning-fast combat, precision platforming, and two opposing worlds collide."
- BRIGANDINE ABYSS (August 27): "The king of Solginat is dead, and a new would-be emperor stands over the corpse. Confront the dark in one of six different storylines as you manage resources, rally your monsters, and stand against the empire."
- Golftacular! (August 27): "Up to 4 players take turns as Tortillo, Chuck, Fin, Poop, Papa, Mama, Claude, and Frend, each one aiming for the hole while unleashing chaos on anyone foolish enough to stand in the way."
- Horripilant (August 27): "Horripilant is a chilling incremental dungeon crawl through the horrors of a forgotten underworld. Combining idler, puzzle and autobattler elements, you’ll fight, mine, and think your way through the depths of a forsaken dungeon."
- Infection Free Zone (August 27): "Type in the name of the city or town, download the map and start playing! Thanks to OpenStreetMap’s real-world data you can choose any place in the world for your survivors."
- Lizards Must Die 2 (August 27): "LIZARDS MUST DIE 2 is a cooperative slasher action game, a high–quality continuation of the SENSATIONAL first part."
- Lou's Lagoon (August 27): "A cozy exploration-and-crafting adventure: fly your seaplane between tropical islands, collect resources with the Swirler, rebuild storm damaged communities, and unravel the mystery surrounding Uncle Lou’s disappearance."
- METAL GEAR SOLID: MASTER COLLECTION Vol.2 (August 27): "Vol. 2 includes Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots and Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker (HD Collection version)."
- Monty The Play Bear (August 27): "Monty The Play Bear is a puzzle game inspired by classic puzzle challenges, featuring a unique continuous movement mechanic. In a toy-filled world, you control Monty, a plush bear, on a journey to reach the castle."

- Tearscape (August 27): "Discover a Gothic world in this 2D top-down action-adventure, blending fast-paced combat, exploration, and pixel art inspired by Game Boy Color classics."

- Whisper Of The House (August 27): "Welcome to Whisper Town—a cozy and heartwarming game about decorating, organizing, and uncovering little stories."
- 1964 Operation Velvet Twins (August 28): "1964: Operation Velvet Twins delivers pure retro fun with no filler just tight gameplay, explosive action, and an unmistakable 8-bit flavor."
- CAPTAIN TSUBASA 2: WORLD FIGHTERS (August 28): "The next episode of Tsubasa’s riveting adventure is here! Enjoy the thrill of spectacular soccer actions with 110 playable characters and new sensational super moves."
- INK ENIGMA: Coloring Hidden Objects (August 28): "Bring the world to life, one discovery at a time. INK ENIGMA: Coloring Hidden Objects takes the classic hidden object genre and gives it a deeply satisfying twist."
- Jonah Lomu Rugby Challenge 4 Remastered (August 28): "Enhanced in stunning 4K with massively upgraded visuals, improved lighting and smooth 60 FPS gameplay on modern hardware."
- Mighty Aphid: Remastered Edition (August 28): "Explore huge levels. Fight big bosses. Earn upgrades. Relive the early days of 2D platform gaming with this modern action-adventure game."
- Once Alive (August 28): "Sixteen years have passed since humanity’s extinction due to a global virus outbreak. You play as James, who, along with his brother, believes they are the last survivors."

- Splash of Color (August 28): "Piece together bright, colorful images by swapping tiles and solving lively puzzles. Watch patterns shift, colors click into place, and pictures slowly reveal themselves as you play."
Xbox Game Pass Titles
- Aerial_Knight's DropShot (August 25) - new to XGP Premium only
- Blood Dungeon (August 25)

Additionally, Xbox Game Pass is adding new titles to its lineup, highlighted by the day-one launch of Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy. The week's schedule spans a wide variety of genres, from action-adventure and shooters to cozy decorating games and retro-inspired platformers.
key_points: Over 30 games are scheduled for release on Xbox between August 24 and August 28.
Highlighted upcoming titles include Aliens: Fireteam Elite 2, Once Human, and the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2.
Xbox Game Pass is receiving new additions such as Blood Dungeon and the day-one launch of Resonance: A Plague Tale Legacy.
The release lineup covers diverse genres, offering everything from intense survival shooters and tactical games to relaxing puzzle and hidden object experiences.

title: 2026 Polestar 3 Performance Review: Faster, Smarter, Better
author: James Morris
content:
The Polestar 3 hit global markets in 2024, and now it’s already had a refresh. Externally, not much has changed. But underneath, there has been major upheaval. I took the top-of-the-range 2026 Polestar 3 Performance for a week-long test and concluded that this is one of the most accomplished electric SUVs on the market.
Polestar 3 Goes 800V
The most fundamental change is that instead of the original car’s 400V architecture, the new version uses an 800V one. That may seem like a technical detail, but it has several positive implications. First, with an 800V system charging times can be considerably quicker. Then there is generally higher efficiency, and potentially the ability to deliver greater motor power.
The new 2026 Polestar 3 benefits in all three areas. The Performance version I borrowed now has 680hp driving all four wheels, where the 2024 model “only” had 517hp. This means it can accelerate to 60mph in a staggeringly quick 3.8 seconds, 0.9 seconds faster than before. That’s insane for a car that weighs 2.5 metric tons. There are similar improvements with the non-Performance versions of the 2026 Polestar 3.
Surprisingly, the battery has gotten a bit smaller. The Performance now has 106kWh (102kWh net), as does the Dual Motor, down from 111kWh (107kWh net). The Single Motor Rear Wheel Drive now offers 92kWh, when before it had the same capacity as the other members of the range. Despite these reduced battery sizes, the range has gone up, from 348 to 373 miles for the Performance, thanks to noticeably improved efficiency. Another benefit of the smaller battery is that the Polestar 3 Performance now weighs 2,525kg instead of 2,584kg.
Polestar 3: Still A Practical Family SUV
Before we get to one of the other most significant improvements, a few words on what was already good – the Polestar 3’s physical characteristics. This is a large SUV, measuring 4.9m (193 inches) in length – more than a Tesla Model Y. But it’s also fairly low at 1.6m (63.5 inches) and the design is sleek. This is no slopey-backed coupe, but it still manages to look extremely sporty. The black car with privacy glass I had for testing was fierce and menacing, with a strong sense of presence and character. The yellow seatbelts, golden brake calipers and gold tire valve covers add to the sense of specialness.
But this is still an incredibly practical car. The cockpit is spacious, and there is a huge amount of room for rear passengers too, with tons of legroom. The headroom is great too, accentuated by the huge panoramic sunroof, which has a £1,600 ($2,200) electrochromatic option that sadly wasn’t included with my test car. My rear passengers mentioned the seats being a little hard for a long journey, but we spent two six-hour journeys in the vehicle so the Polestar 3 was facing steep odds in the comfort category.
Despite the sporty aim, the Polestar 3 also has plenty of rear cargo space. With the rear seats up, you get a reasonable 484 liters, which extends to 1,411 liters with them down. The rear seats only have a 60-40 split, but the 60% portion at least has a built-in ski hatch. There’s a 32-liter frunk as well. The rear cargo space floor is a little high, but 90 liters of the rear capacity are under the floor – more than adequate for charging cables. The parcel shelf design uses a retractable blind and is easy to operate. There’s a hefty 2,200kg braked (750kg unbraked) towing capacity, too, with an electrically retractable tow bar that is a £1,200 extra.
Faster Polestar 3 Computing
This brings us to the other major under-the-hood upgrade with the Polestar 3 – a much more powerful central computer. The 2024 car’s NVIDIA DRIVE Xavier delivered 30 trillion operations per second (TOPS). Now the 2026 model’s NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Orin offers 254 TOPS, an over eight times increase. This theoretically will enable much more sophisticated ADAS functions and even some self-driving ability, although vehicles that major on this such as the XPENG L03 have even more – 2,250 TOPS in the case of the L03 Ultra.
Button lovers won’t be entirely enamored with the Polestar 3, however. It does have conventional stalks for wipers, lights and drive controls. There’s a knob for media control too. But everything else goes via the infotainment screen. This means that climate control adjustments beyond temperature and fan speed are best performed by a passenger, as they are fiddly to access when driving. Worst of all, window demisting is not immediately available. Luckily, Google Assistant is effective for operating these via voice.
Another slight flaw is that the wireless charging pad is off by default, requiring it to be turned on every time the car is started. The pad is also shallow, so that your phone will slide off under hard acceleration. There’s a clear head-up display, but I found the speed limit notifications could sometimes be wrong, a problem not exclusive to many cars that use road sign recognition. On the plus side, the optional 1.3Mpixel HD LED headlights are adaptive and truly excellent. They certainly facilitated navigating dark single-track lanes in Devon, and are a recommended £1,600 ($2,200) extra.
Polestar 3 Driving And Range
The whole point of the Polestar brand as a counterpoint to its sibling Volvo is driving experience. The latter is supposed to be the safe family option. I’ve driven the other members of the Polestar 3 range, and while they handle well, the Performance variant is on a different level. It has Polestar’s trick active air suspension, which combines dual-chamber air springs with ZF active dampers. These can supposedly adjust 500 times per second. The system drops the car down slightly at speed to reduce drag, and keeps things level if the loading is uneven. Best of all, though, is how it handles bumpy roads. We’re not quite talking Range Rover air suspension here, but the ride quality is still one of the best I’ve experienced. Yet it’s also stiff enough for flat cornering.
In Performance mode with everything stiffened up, the Polestar 3 is an absolute hooligan. The acceleration is almost as brutal as a Tesla Performance car, and the steering surprisingly nimble and assured. But this is also an exceptional highway cruiser, with tons of torque for high-speed overtaking while feeling completely planted. When you get stuck in traffic jams or average speed zones, the Adaptive Cruise Control with lane centering does a great job of keeping you a safe distance from the car in front, while steering round corners automatically. In my six-hour trip to Devon, it was a godsend. In other words, this car is a brilliant long-range mile muncher, and it has the range to back that up too.
On paper, the Polestar 3 Performance has a WLTP range of 373 miles. During my testing on a wide selection of roads, but the majority motorways and A-roads with a 60mph limit, I managed an average of 2.7 miles per kWh, which would imply a real-world range of 275 miles. While this isn’t super-efficient, it’s much better than many performance electric SUVs I’ve tested. The superb Lotus Eletre only managed 2.1 miles per kWh when I tried that a few years ago. I wasn’t making much of an effort to save energy, either, because you don’t buy a Polestar 3 Performance to drive slowly.
This is matched by how good the Polestar is at replenishing its battery. While the original car was no charging slouch, hitting a maximum of 250kW, the new version maxes out at 350kW. I tested my loaner on a new IONITY 400kW charger and saw 319kW at 37% capacity, and even at 60% capacity the rate was still 168kW. Despite the huge battery, this car only takes 22 minutes to go from 10-80%. Combined with the decent range, this rapid charging makes the Polestar 3 Performance a very capable long-distance car, albeit maybe not to BMW iX3 or Volvo EX60 levels. When I drove from London to South Devon (and back), the car could have done all 243 miles easily on a single 100% charge, but stopping was no hardship with such rapid charging.
Polestar 3: Fast, Practical, But Expensive
Overall, there’s little to fault with the Polestar 3 Performance. It’s ridiculously quick and engaging to drive in the most powerful Performance mode, and it’s still quick enough even in Range mode. The ride quality is superb, and there’s tons of space for passengers and cargo. It’s big but not a complete liability on narrow country roads and in urban environments. The one caveat is the price. At the time of writing, there was a £10,000 ($13,600) discount until the end of September, yet you’ll still need to part with at least £82,040 ($112,000).
That pushes it way above the leader in this class, the Tesla Model Y, and will naturally keep sales volume low. The BMW iX3 and Volvo EX60 give you more range but less performance for less money. But the Polestar 3 Performance is still an enticingly complete package, combining driving pleasure with family practicality and long-distance capability. All this is bad news for American car buyers, because in June Polestar pulled out of the USA due to the country’s legislation targeting cars manufactured in China. So this superb premium SUV won’t be available to Americans, which is a shame for such a great all-conquering electric car.
summary: The 2026 Polestar 3 Performance features a major architecture upgrade from 400V to 800V, boosting power to 680hp and improving both charging speeds and efficiency. Despite having a slightly smaller battery than the 2024 model, its range has increased to 373 miles, and it can charge from 10% to 80% in just 22 minutes. The vehicle combines sports-car acceleration and active air suspension with family-friendly practicality, ample cargo space, and a high-end central computer.
key_points: The 2026 Polestar 3 shifts to an 800V architecture, enabling faster charging up to 350kW and increased motor power up to 680hp for the Performance model.
Despite a reduced battery capacity, efficiency improvements raise the WLTP range to 373 miles for the Performance variant.
The central computer has been upgraded from the NVIDIA DRIVE Xavier to the NVIDIA DRIVE AGX Orin, increasing performance from 30 to 254 TOPS.
The car offers a spacious cabin, 484 liters of rear cargo space, a 32-liter frunk, and a 2,200kg braked towing capacity.
The Polestar 3 Performance is priced high starting at least £82,040 ($112,000) and will not be available in the United States.

title: Fenix 9 might launch on 25 August - Details
author: The
content:
![Garmin Fenix 8 Pro MicroLED smartwatch, first look](https://imagedelivery.net/_jGo7Cp8DLHLbI9FzBn6-Q/the5krunner.com/2025/09/garmin-fenix-8-pro-review-first-look-microled.png/w=9999)
Garmin’s August 25 Livestream: What We Expect
Garmin has scheduled a YouTube launch event for Tuesday, August 25, at 12 PM UK time, titled “Play Harder”. The video’s thumbnail teaser shows a surfer and the tagline “engineered on the inside for life on the outside.”
We expect four watches and a total of at least nine size variants:
| Model | Display | Expected size(s) | Confidence based on prior leaks | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Enduro 4 | MIP-Solar only | 51mm | Moderate–high | 
| Fenix 9 | AMOLED | 43mm, 47mm, 51mm | Moderate | 
| Fenix 9 | MIP-Solar | 43mm, 47mm, 51mm | Moderate | 
| Fenix E2 | AMOLED only | 43mm, 47mm | Moderate | 
Edit: A source with direct visibility from a Garmin employee says “43mm is on all Fenix models this time round.” That would mean Garmin has solved the antenna and solar-panel packaging limits that kept 43mm off MIP-Solar in the previous generation and sees enough demand for a smaller E2.
For the reasoning behind each of these, see our Fenix E2, 9 AMOLED, 9 MIP Solar, Pro and Enduro filings analysis. The timing lines up with Garmin’s own second quarter 2026 results, in which the company pointed to a launch-heavy second half for its Outdoor division, and with the FCC filings for Garmin International.
A dedicated livestream is rare for Garmin, which normally announces new hardware by press release. The only precedent is the Fenix 8, Fenix E, and Enduro 3 launch on 27 August 2024, which also had its own livestream page. Repeating that format two years later confirms this site’s view that it must, at minimum, be a Fenix 9 launch.

Expected announcements include four new watch models spanning at least nine size variants, such as the Enduro 4, Fenix 9, and Fenix E2. This rare livestream format for Garmin strongly indicates a major hardware launch following previous FCC filings and second-quarter financial results.

Expected releases include the Enduro 4, Fenix 9, and Fenix E2 models across multiple sizes.

title: Please don't buy Google's wildly overpriced Pixel 11 Clear Case
author: Will Sattelberg
content:
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/08/Pixel-11-clear-case-and-in-Olive.jpg?quality=82&strip=all&w=1600) 
Buying a new smartphone usually means buying a new case alongside it, unless you’re one of those risk-fueled daredevils who opt to go caseless. And while there’s no shortage of third-party case options piling up at your local Best Buy or in Amazon warehouses, sometimes, going the first-party route just makes sense — especially if you’re able to pick one up with store credit. If you’re salivating over the new Pixel 11 series, I beg of you: please don’t choose Google’s wildly overpriced Pixelsnap Clear Case. It’s simply not worth the cost.
I’m a little picky (okay, very picky) when it comes to phone cases, which I know puts me in the minority among general smartphone shoppers. But even if you’re the kind of person who opts for a clear shell rather than something with a little more character, Google’s Pixel 11 Clear Case just isn’t it. I have actual critiques about the case itself, but I think I can convince most shoppers to stay away with a single number: $50. That’s the same price as the colorful (and still not very good) Pixel cases Google’s been selling for a few years now, and only $25 less than Bellroy’s leather wallet case for the Pixel 11 Pro Fold, which, if you didn’t know, uses genuine leather.
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/08/MBG-Pixel-11-clear-case-2.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
If you’re still looking for reasons not to pick this up, don’t worry — I have more ammo than just the price tag. Google’s offering doesn’t elevate the experience above any other generic TPU-based shell. If I’m being generous, you could argue that official Pixelsnap support could elevate its magnetic grip over third-party rivals, but I can’t say I’ve noticed a difference. Save for the circular support magnet, this feels virtually identical to this Spigen offering that is currently up on Amazon for $15 (or $17 for Pro XL users).
Actually, that’s not entirely true — Spigen’s is probably better. While the left and right sides of Spigen’s case do have a little more flex than Google’s (something that won’t matter once it’s on the phone), Google’s case leaves the entire bottom gap effectively unprotected. I’m not saying it’s guaranteed, but I wouldn’t be surprised if a drop at an unlucky angle could leave your Pixel 11’s display shattered or the surrounding frame nicked. Google’s case is also noticeably yellower than Spigen’s, even right out of the box, and considering that all clear TPU cases eventually oxidize, you’re probably better off starting with one that’s at least making an effort.
![](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/4/2026/08/Pixel-11-clear-case-cutout-1.jpg?quality=82&strip=all)
This isn’t an appeal to specifically buy Spigen’s clear case; it’s simply the go-to third party default for most phones these days. Rather, this is simultaneously a PSA to Pixel shoppers not to go with first-party case offerings, and a plea to Google to step up its absolutely lackluster case designs. Despite growing success, Pixel users still lack the breadth and depth of options that the iPhone and Samsung’s flagship devices see with every generation. It’s getting better, but in the meantime, it would be great to have a solid option from Google to point at during a hardware launch. Ah well — maybe the Pixel 12 will fare better.
More on Pixel 11:
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-dark.png) 
![Add 9to5Google as a preferred source on Google](https://9to5google.com/wp-content/themes/ninetofive/dist/images/google-preferred-source-badge-light.png)
summary: The author advises Pixel 11 buyers to avoid Google's Pixelsnap Clear Case, arguing that it is overpriced at $50 and lacks quality compared to alternatives. The first-party case features a generic TPU build, leaves the bottom of the phone unprotected, and exhibits a yellowish tint right out of the box. Cheaper third-party options, such as Spigen's clear case, offer better value and protection.
key_points: Google's Pixel 11 Clear Case costs $50, making it wildly overpriced for what it offers.
The case feels like a generic TPU shell and leaves the entire bottom of the phone unprotected.
Google's clear case is noticeably yellower than competing options right out of the box.
Third-party alternatives, such as Spigen's case, are significantly cheaper and perform better.
